              A question must identify its subject as well as show a board. This knight lesson uses a 29×10
              display frame containing an 8×8 board and a separate 8×8 answer grid, or mask, below it. A footer between
              them names the side, selected piece, square and question type.
            
              Here the footer selects the
              first-side knight at board row 7, column 1, or b1 in the added chess coordinates. The question asks for legal destinations. The knight can move to
              a3 and c3. Its jump also reaches d2 geometrically, but a friendly pawn
              occupies that square.
            
              Document 3, trace 3068, step 33. Within this 29×10 display frame, the board occupies rows
              1–8 and columns 1–8; the mask occupies rows 11–18 and columns
              1–8; the footer is row 9. Coordinates start at 0. The mask’s plus-shaped glyph 5
              marks indices 40 and 42 within the 8×8 mask, corresponding to a3 and c3. This illustration shows the stored answer.
            
An ordinary capture removes the opposing piece at the destination and puts the moving piece there. A friendly piece prevents a move to that square. A legal move must also leave its own king safe. An attack on the king is check; check with no legal escape is checkmate. The king stays on the board when the game ends.
King safety depends on the resulting position. In one course example, a king on e1 tries to capture a bishop on d1 while an opposing rook stands on f1. Before the move, the king itself blocks the rook’s line to d1. Once the king leaves e1, that line opens, so the capture is illegal. The course shows the attempted move’s resulting occupancy and attack. Testing a king capture means moving the king, removing the captured piece, and checking its destination in that changed position.
Controlled squares and legal moves
Control follows a piece’s movement geometry in the displayed position. For a rook, bishop or queen, it extends along each permitted straight line to the first occupied square, including a friendly piece it defends. Pins do not remove controlled squares. Here the bishop on b5 points along a diagonal through the knight on c6 toward the knight’s king on e8. Moving the knight would expose the king. The knight still controls eight squares, but has no legal destination.
The control question follows the knight’s jump pattern. The legal-move question also checks whether moving would expose its king. The course distinguishes these questions with different mode glyphs. The board stays the same; the empty legal-move mask and eight-square control mask are answers to different questions. This knight cannot move along the diagonal that pins it. A pinned sliding piece or pawn can sometimes move along its pin line while continuing to shield its king, so a pin does not always mean that a piece has no legal move.
              Control mask: document 3, trace 3124, step 1. Legal-move mask: trace 3119, step 8. Both show
              the same board and selected knight.
            
Learning how moves are packed
              A numeric table provides values, but their meaning must also be taught. Document 4 explains how a move’s
              origin square, destination square and promotion choice form a packed number. These lessons are part of the
              payload and become accessible through the reader established by the bootstrap.
            
              One stored example uses origin 52,
              destination 36 and
              choice 0: e2→e4 without promotion. Squares are numbered across rows from a8=0 to h8=7, continuing
              down to a1=56. Choice 0 means no promotion; 1, 2, 3 and 4 select queen, rook,
              bishop and knight.
            
Both before-and-after boards already appear in the source display. The two crops below show the numeric part of that display before and after a trace step fills in the packed result. The board pictures do not move between these two states.
52, 36, 0; packed-word row blank26912
              Document 4, page 1076→trace 1075. The crops show display-frame rows 9–11 and columns
              0–18. A bit 0 uses glyph 2, the decimal digit 0 uses glyph 22, and
              a blank cell uses glyph 0. These are three distinct records.
            
              The completed word is 0110100100100000 = 26,912, calculated as 52×512 + 36×8 + 0. Its fields are one leading zero, six origin bits, six
              destination bits and three choice bits. Other stored examples unpack a word into these fields and reject a
              leading 1 or a choice outside 0–4.
            
              The table [16,1,6,6,3] describes those widths: 16 bits total, with fields of
              1, 6, 6 and 3 bits. The pictures teach which fields mean padding, origin, destination and
              choice. The table alone provides widths, not that interpretation. We can now use the same rule to
              understand a move in the anthology.
            
A well-formed move word is not necessarily a legal move. Packing checks field ranges; unpacking also rejects a nonzero leading bit. Neither operation checks the board, whose turn it is, or whether promotion is possible. Those questions require the chess rules and the position’s state.
Following one move from source to display
              The first game in the anthology has 52 individual moves, or plies, beginning with d2→d4.
              The byte-to-picture walkthrough above recovered this game’s initial frame. Following its first
              move now connects the stored number’s meaning to the separately stored display update. The anthology stores the move in two
              forms: a numeric move word and a display patch. The recipient must recover them separately and learn why they describe the same move.
            
1. Produce the move word and display patch
              Game preparation starts with the anthology in PGN, a human-readable notation for recorded games.
              The source importer checks each game’s main line by replaying it legally from the standard
              starting position. It records every intermediate board, the side to move, and each move’s
              origin, destination and explicit promotion choice. The first move here gives
              [51,35,0]. Packing gives 51×512 + 35×8 = 26,392, stored as bytes
              103 24.
            
              The same replay supplies the board before and after the move. Comparing their display cells produces three
              assignments: place pawn glyph 32 at cell 35,
              clear cell 51 to glyph 0, and change footer cell 64 from side glyph 3 to side glyph 4. The move
              word and patch come from this common replay. The reader does not calculate one from the other.
            
The message builder loads the checked game and presentation data, packs the move tables, and assembles the document. It verifies the retained inputs before using them. This construction uses the qualified presentation data rather than reimporting the PGN on every build.
              The authoring code shares identical glyphs, frames and tables between games, then assigns trace IDs. In
              document 2, trace 324 refers to initial frame 256, move table 257 and score table 258. Packing adds schema
              table 388 as another reference. These IDs identify objects only within this document.
            
257 was a trace; document 2’s 257 is a table. Miniature 256 and document 2’s 256 are also
              different frames. A name never identifies a record across document boundaries.
            2. Store the document in a checked section
              Document 2 contains 93,017 bytes. Its six-byte section header is
              0 2 | 0 1 107 89: section ID 2 and body length 93,017. CRC-32C over that header
              and body gives 182 147 233 40. Adding the four check bytes gives a 93,027-byte
              section.
            
              The section starts at stream byte 13,533, which maps to physical row 116, column 1,768. Its
              body starts six bytes later, at stream byte 13,539. The boundary falls inside a physical row:
              section storage follows the byte stream continuously, without row packets or row separators.
            
3. Recover and validate document 2
              The recipient finds this boundary by reading the inventory section and document 1’s section
              lengths. The inventory declares document ID 2, body length 93,017, expected check
              182 147 233 40 and 64 entry IDs, starting with 324. These declarations must match the received
              section and document header.
            
              The document header starts 214 57 | 0 64 | 0 151: marker, 64 entries and 151 records. Its
              first entry is 1 68, or 324. Reading each length-delimited record builds a map from IDs to
              records. Resolving trace 324 then finds frame 256 and tables 257, 258 and 388. Schema 388 is
              near the document’s end, so references must work even when the target record occurs later.
            
257 and trace 324: actual record bytes
              Spaces in these transcripts separate fields for reading; they are not stored delimiters. The table’s
              payload length, 109 bytes, and its row count, 52, are different fields.
            
4. Locate and read the first move word
              Table 257 starts at document byte 438. Its seven-byte record header is followed by a four-byte row count
              and a one-byte column count. Its first value therefore begins at byte 450 and occupies bytes 450–451.
            
              The document body starts at stream byte 13,539. Adding 450 locates the first value at stream
              bytes 13,989–13,990. Frame 16’s mapping places its sixteen bits at physical row
              118, columns 1,320–1,335. They read 0110011100011000: bytes 103 and
              24, giving 103×256+24 = 26,392.
            
              Read the sixteen positions from left to right: 0110011100011000. The table keeps those same
              bits visible while showing their readings.
            
5. Interpret the move fields
              Apply schema 388 using the meanings taught in document 4: 0 | 110011 | 100011 | 000. The
              fields give padding 0, origin 51, destination 35 and choice 0: d2→d4 without promotion. These
              square numbers use row-major order on the 8×8 board; they are distinct from coordinates in the physical
              message.
            
              The table reader recovers the value 26,392. Interpreting it as a chess move requires
              the course’s explanation of the fields. The native player does not use this word to calculate a legal
              board update; it displays the separately stored patch.
            
6. Apply the stored patch
              Trace 324’s first patch occupies document bytes 15,048–15,058:
              0 3 | 0 35 32 | 0 51 0 | 0 64 4. The count is three, followed by assignments (cell 35, glyph
              32), (cell 51, glyph 0) and (cell 64, glyph 4). Two change board cells; the third changes the
              footer’s turn marker.
            
              Both before and after the patch, glyph 32 refers to the same bitmap recovered earlier:
              a 5×5 picture with mask bytes 1 8 64 0. The patch changes where it is drawn.
              The glyph record itself stays unchanged.
            
Record 32 → a 5×5 bitmap
                00000 / 00100 / 00100 / 00100 / 00000
              
The first 25 bits of bytes 1, 8, 64, 0, across each row and then down.
256, board region1 · d2 empty, pawn on d4
              The frame is 9×8; these pictures crop its first eight rows. Cell 64 is outside the board and is shown
              separately in the complete replay below. Colored areas identify the assigned board cells.
            
The two stored representations agree: the move word specifies d2→d4, and the patch moves the pawn between those squares while changing the turn marker. During message creation, the program checks the reconstructed pictures against the board positions obtained from the original game’s moves. A recipient who has learned the meanings can compare them; the player itself only looks up glyphs and assigns cell values.
The move word, patch and bitmap thus meet in one displayed change. The bootstrap supplies the operations needed to recover and draw it; the course supplies its chess meaning. The special moves below use the same operations, with additional rules determining which changes are valid.
Why board positions need history
The first move changes two board cells and a footer. Other moves depend on more information or change additional squares. The course teaches these cases by showing a position, an attempted move and its result, then comparing what happens when a relevant condition changes.
              In the examples below, the before-and-after boards occupy two regions of one stored display frame, at
              display-frame columns 0–7 and 9–16. They are not separate frame records. The crops show only
              the squares needed to explain each rule.
            
Castling moves two pieces
In this king-side castling example, the king and rook leave e1 and h1 and arrive on g1 and f1. Four board cells change. Castling requires the corresponding right to remain and every square between king and rook to be empty. The king must be safe on its starting square, its transit square after leaving the start, and its destination after both pieces move. The course compares accepted castling with attempts that fail these conditions.
A king or rook that moves and returns does not recover its lost right. For queen-side castling, the square next to the rook must also be empty, though the king never crosses it. An attack on that square or on the rook itself does not prevent castling; the safety test concerns the king’s route.
4, trace 798, step 0. The crops show e1–h1 in the before-and-after board regions.
              The first side also loses its castling rights after this move.
            En passant depends on the immediately preceding move
Immediately after the opposing pawn advances from d7 to d5, the pawn on e5 can capture on d6. That destination was empty. The captured pawn is removed from d5, so three squares change. The crop shows d6 and e6 above d5 and e5.
A matched example moves both sides’ knights away and back, restoring the same board occupancy. The opportunity for en passant has expired, so the same attempted capture is refused and the board remains unchanged. The pieces alone do not record when the opposing pawn advanced.
En passant must also leave the moving side’s king safe. Removing both pawns from their original squares can open an attacking line. The course includes an immediate capture refused for this reason, even though its timing and pawn geometry are otherwise correct.
4, trace 906. Step 0 shows the available capture; step 4 shows the same board after
              the opportunity has expired.
            Promotion needs a separate choice
              Here the pawn leaves b7, captures the
              rook on a8, and is replaced by the
              selected promotion piece. Choice 1 produces a queen;
              choice 4 produces a knight. Both moves have the same origin and destination, so the promotion choice needs
              its own field. The course also shows rook and bishop promotion and rejects a missing promotion choice.
            
1: queen a8; b7 empty4: knight a8; b7 empty4, trace 929, steps 0 and 9. Each crop shows a8 and b8 above a7 and b7.
            History is part of the state
              A king can leave its starting square and return, restoring the board and side to move while losing
              castling rights. Document 4, trace 1000 at step 3, compares two matching boards with
              different histories: the first side has both castling rights in one case and neither in the other.
            
Repetition uses a precise meaning of “the same position”: the pieces occupy the same squares, the same side is to move, castling rights match, and any legal en-passant opportunity matches. An en-passant target counts only if an actual legal capture is available. A target that no pawn can use, or that would expose its own king, does not distinguish the position.
Count occurrences of the current position throughout the legal history, including the initial occurrence. They need not be consecutive. A separate counter records plies since the last pawn move or capture; either resets it to zero. That counter affects a draw claim, but is not part of the position compared for repetition.
              The course carries legal histories and state displays for these distinctions. Reused history
              segments have explicit links and complete starting pictures, so opening a segment does not
              require the player to calculate its starting position. The anthology’s 72 display
              cells serve a smaller purpose: its board and footer show play and result, without listing
              all castling rights or an en-passant square.
            
When a game ends
A side with no legal move is checkmated if its king is in check, and stalemated otherwise. Checkmate is a loss; stalemate is a draw. Golden Board also recognizes three classes where neither side can give checkmate: king against king, king and bishop against king, and king and knight against king. Its rules machinery ends play after a legal move reaches one of these board endings, and refuses later moves or declarations.
              A claim for threefold repetition becomes available once the current position has appeared
              at least three times. A fifty-move claim needs at least 100 plies since the last
              pawn move or capture. Neither condition ends play automatically: the side to move must
              explicitly claim the eligible draw. A move that would reach a threshold does not make that
              claim available in advance. The course shows eligible claims and the separate events that
              accept or refuse them.
            
Either side can resign while play is active, awarding the other side the win. Draw agreement requires both sides’ explicit consent after each has made a move. These declarations have known causes. An anthology score only records the outcome: a win or draw on a nonterminal board does not identify resignation, agreement or a claim.
              This is the project’s practical chess profile. It excludes automatic fivefold and
              75-move adjudication, intended-next-move claim procedures, tournament procedures,
              and a general solver for positions where checkmate is impossible. Material outside the
              three recognized dead-position classes receives no general deadness verdict.
            
Tactics, mating and strategic guidance
The later course builds on control and legality to teach attacks, defenses, pins and forks. A fork here is one piece geometrically attacking at least two opposing pieces. That fact alone does not prove that either capture is legal or profitable. A passed pawn has no opposing pawn ahead on its own or an adjacent file; it still faces kings, other pieces and the timing of play.
Mating instruction includes king-and-queen and king-and-rook continuations, with contrasts that end in stalemate. A legal line ending in mate can still depend on the opponent choosing a losing reply. To support a forced win, the winning side may choose its continuations, but every legal defensive move and every eligible defensive draw claim must be covered. All resulting branches must end in the asserted win.
The message carries finite worked examples of this distinction. One starts with White’s king on f3 and queen on h4, and Black’s lone king on g1. White moves the queen to g3. Black’s only legal moves are king g1→f1 and king g1→h1. The stored continuations answer the first with queen g3→f2 and the second with queen g3→g2; both give checkmate. Covering only one reply would leave the forced-win claim incomplete. The player presents these stored displays and tables without searching for a mating line.
              Strategic lessons use observable facts such as development, central control, open files
              and mobility. Their rough material scale assigns 1 to a pawn, 3 to a
              knight or bishop, 5 to a rook and 9 to a queen; the king has no exchange
              value. These counts and comparisons provide guidance, not a verdict on the better position
              or best move. A worked move-check routine first establishes whether play is active, whose
              turn it is, whether the king is in check, and which draw claims are available. It then
              examines legal choices and the shown move’s effects, including captures, check and game
              endings. Comparisons remain limited to the continuations actually supplied.
            
Replaying a complete game
              The 52-ply game has 53 display states: its initial frame and the result after each patch. To reconstruct a
              state, copy the initial frame and apply all patches up to that point. Moving backward reconstructs an
              earlier state in the same way; it does not require reversing chess moves.
            
              The board and eight-cell footer appear separately below. Footer cell 0 identifies the side to
              move. In the final patch, footer cell 1 changes to glyph 11, the second-side result mark.
              Score table 258 contains 1, recording a second-side win. This stored result does not imply that the final
              displayed board is checkmate.
            
1: all 53 display states and the footer
              Use Next move to apply the next stored patch, Previous to reconstruct the preceding state, and Reset to
              restore the start. The 53 states cover 0–52 plies.
              Blue areas mark cleared cells;
              ochre areas mark assigned pieces;
              teal areas mark footer changes. The interpreted move word is listed
              separately.
            
1 board · initial position
First side to move; result mark blank.
State 1 of 53 · before any move
Initial frame 256
Move-word details begin with the first stored update.
                  No patch applied. The source picture has 64 board cells and 8 footer cells.
                
The controls inspect stored moves and patches. This page does not calculate chess rules or generate legal moves.
1 · d2→d419 · first side castles52 · final carried board
              The three checkpoints show selected states without interaction. Across 64 games, the artifact stores
              6,890 plies and 6,954 initial-or-updated board states. The game records contain
              no names, dates, opening labels or commentary.
            
The player displays castling, promotion and en passant by applying their stored cell changes. Interpreting move words or deciding whether a new move is legal requires the rules taught by the course. The picture player does neither.
Before you go
Getting from a square of bits to a game takes patience. Thank you for giving so much of your time and attention.
If something is unclear, seems wrong, or could be explained better, please let me know. Questions, corrections and other ideas are welcome, whether they concern the Golden Board itself or this guide.
You're also welcome to build on the source code. Try another subject, another way of teaching it, or a different experiment.
If you share or adapt the project, or use it in research, please credit and link the original work; the repository includes a BibTeX citation.
I'd love to see what you make from it.

articles.title: The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over
articles.body:
The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over
“Life was simpler on Active Directory, at least I could manage every identity”.
I made that quote up, but there is nostalgia for a golden age of corporate IT that’s never coming back: Many enterprises still (try to) track identities in Active Directory (AD), a service that’s old enough to drink and crumbles at the scale of modern cloud computing.
It held up because the architecture is simple enough: Active Directory is an LDAP directory to store identities and a Kerberos implementation to let them authenticate, wrapped in decent UX and with continued updates.
AD accomplished the goal of identity management: A way to know all identities, who vouched for them, and where they’re valid. It answered three questions in a unified catalog:
- What identities exist? With the directory, which records every user and machine
- What vouched for the identity? With a domain controller that approves authentication based on admin credentials
- Where is the identity valid? With AD domain architecture that reflects the company’s infrastructure
Security policies are moot if you can't answer any one of them. I spent many hours keeping our Active Directory catalog accurate so it could answer these questions, because everything downstream depended on it: issuing certificates automatically with Certificate Services, applying settings at scale with Group Policies, and more.
There were always some compromises: databases with local users, Linux servers requiring workarounds (Thank you SSSD!), but most users and machines in my network had an identity in Active Directory, and I knew which didn’t.
But unifying every identity in Active Directory (or any one directory) is nearly impossible with modern cloud architecture. There’s an AD ecosystem of security products, password rotations, and sync plugins that modernizes it, but nothing can undo architecture choices from a bygone era.
Active Directory is the new mainframe: great for its time, but you’d never choose to start from scratch. Replacing it is impossible because it’s so entrenched.
Active Directory can accurately reflect human identities with a few integrations and plugins, but machine identities are nearly impossible.
Maybe that’s controversial. You can come to me with torches, pitchforks, and architectural diagrams about Kubernetes pod identity attestation in AD, but Active Directory is still a piece of infrastructure built for a bygone era.
Visibility and attestation: Unified machine identity is nearly impossible in Active Directory
Most organizations are creating grave security risks because they don’t understand modern machine identity. I once spoke to someone at a conference who told me they had recently discovered a publicly exposed Lambda function. Bad enough, but that function’s policy was iam:* meaning it could take any IAM action, including crowning any attacker the organization’s superadmin. Oh, and by the way, this was a defense organization.
If an organization with high security requirements makes these blunders, you don’t want to know what happens at other organizations. This problem isn’t specific to AD, but it is a symptom of organizations not figuring out how to correctly attest machine identity in modern software development.
To understand why no organization can account for all of its machine identities in AD, we need to understand how a machine enters a domain. A domain is an administrative boundary that shares security rules. In practice, this is usually an organization.
When a new machine joins your domain, three main events happen:
- An object is created inside the directory (often called a machine account)
- DNS is updated, certificates are issued (assuming you have AD Certificate Services autoenrollment)
- Kerberos tickets are issued so the machine can assert its identity
When that machine logs in, it authenticates to a Domain Controller (the server running Active Directory for the domain), which trusts it because the machine is in its directory. But the machine had to enter the directory first.
When Active Directory was built, that meant a human manually added it. “Machines” were physical servers that got delivered to the office, installed in the server dungeon room, and registered by a human admin.
Human approval doesn’t scale to developers creating and deprecating testing databases, Kubernetes clusters, and CI runners at will. Contemporary AD implementations deal with this by deferring authority. An admin token (sometimes hardcoded…) automatically joins new identities.
Using human credentials to join new machines is a workaround that negates the point: Admin approval implies a human can tell you about each trusted device.
No admin can know every EC2 instance, PostgreSQL database, or CI runner in the organization. This is also because when AD was built, machine identities were long-lived devices, not ephemeral cloud resources.
Active Directory was built for human approval of long-lived infrastructure, but now often auto-approves short-lived cloud resources.
Even if you built all of the complex automations to reflect every testing database and Kubernetes pod in AD with automated admin approval, it’s security theater. The unified directory would exist on paper, but lack authority.
Modern cloud infrastructure automatically asserts machine identity:
- In Kubernetes, each pod gets a service account token, which allows it to assert its identity within the cluster.
- In Azure, you can configure a machine identity in Entra ID and let Azure’s Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) automatically issue OAuth tokens when machines request them.
These two examples have modern assumptions baked in: machines need to self-serve their identities when they’re spun up. They also assume a narrow scope.
Scope: how identity perimeters have changed
The unified directory of identity management aimed to encompass every device, user, and piece of infrastructure. Authenticating to the Domain Controller would be enough to get access to everything a user/machine needs and nothing they don’t.
This is the identity perimeter: where an identity is valid. In the Active Directory era, the perimeter was as large as possible. The more complete the perimeter, the more authoritative the directory. As an example, SQL Server accepts Windows authentication (i.e. an AD identity) or SQL authentication (username and password). Active Directory admins choose Windows auth to keep the perimeter large.
Anything outside of the directory would be a “shadow identity”: a valid identity that grants access to corporate infrastructure, but isn’t accounted for in identity management (unless you consider the post-it note on my monitor identity management).
A separate username-password set creates a separate perimeter. This used to be a problem, but is now the norm. Each API key, database string, or auth token creates a separate perimeter because they’re a credential that represents an identity for just one service. As an example, GitHub automation requires personal access tokens or GitHub private keys and doesn’t work with any directory identity.
But just to make it harder, zero-trust architecture makes machines constantly authenticate to each other, which skyrockets the count of credentials and creates hundreds of perimeters.
In theory, a small perimeter shrinks the blast radius of any breach: A compromised Notion session token should only give Notion access. In practice, an attacker may find additional credentials in Notion, which lets them expand their access. Oh, and the physical security layer of firewalls and physical perimeters is gone in the cloud era, so a leaked credential works from any attacker’s laptop.
This should concern admins more than it does: many teams keep troves of sensitive plaintext credentials in .env files or hardcode them in configuration files. The response is often lackluster:
- Use SSO where it’s available for human users
- Teach the team how to securely handle plaintext machine credentials
A solution like Active Directory is nearly useless for solving these issues.
The new paradigm
Organizations can tame the complexity of machine identity in the cloud, but not as simply as one massive Active Directory list. Instead, we see two main vectors to fix this:
The first is identity federation, where one platform trusts another platform’s approval to authenticate a workload. All three major clouds support this.
Using OpenID Connect (OIDC), AWS can sign a token for an EC2 instance to access PostgreSQL in Azure. Entra federated credentials natively support this use case and would trust the EC2 workload.
This works for many use cases. If you’re exclusively on AWS and run Terraform from GitHub Actions, OIDC federation straight into IAM does the job: You get visibility, know why you trust it, and know its scope. But it’s laborious to implement each relationship, which means it relies on IAM administrators who can barely keep up with group membership requests. Moreover, if said pipeline is breached by, say, a supply chain attack (which are common nowadays), the whole perimeter is breached.
Even if your admins are bored, no cloud has native bridges between every possible tool, so federation stops as soon as any service only accepts an API key. Organizations shouldn’t accept unruly, long-standing plaintext credentials outside of security purview.
That’s why organizations adopt a brokering approach. Here, credentials live in a secrets manager like Infisical (which securely stores and then delivers secrets to workloads at runtime). This creates a meta-perimeter for all of those micro-perimeters. Infisical (or another tool) acts like a broker: Machines authenticate to it, they broker access to the credential store, and inject the credentials the identity can read into its runtime.
These two patterns can bring order to the Wild West of machine identity in the cloud era. They check the boxes Active Directory once did:
- What identities exist? You have an overview of who authenticates and what they do
- What vouched for the identity? You know where workloads originate and why they’re trusted without relying on a human to approve everything
- Where is the identity valid? Keys, tokens, and strings have a natural perimeter.
This is especially important as organizations increasingly adopt AI agents, which often need their own identities, separate security policies, and even separate security tooling. Getting machine identity right is more important than ever. If you can’t keep track of testing databases and a Stripe API key, you don’t want autonomous software that can create its own databases and send that API key to strangers online.

Most organizations are creating grave security risks because they don’t understand modern machine identity. I once spoke to someone at a conference who told me they had recently discovered a publicly exposed Lambda function. Bad enough, but that function’s policy was iam:* meaning it could take any IAM action, including crowning any attacker the organization’s superadmin. Oh, and by the way, this was a defense organization.
If an organization with high security requirements makes these blunders, you don’t want to know what happens at other organizations. This problem isn’t specific to AD, but it is a symptom of organizations not figuring out how to correctly attest machine identity in modern software development.
To understand why no organization can account for all of its machine identities in AD, we need to understand how a machine enters a domain. A domain is an administrative boundary that shares security rules. In practice, this is usually an organization.
When a new machine joins your domain, three main events happen:
- An object is created inside the directory (often called a machine account)
- DNS is updated, certificates are issued (assuming you have AD Certificate Services autoenrollment)
- Kerberos tickets are issued so the machine can assert its identity
When that machine logs in, it authenticates to a Domain Controller (the server running Active Directory for the domain), which trusts it because the machine is in its directory. But the machine had to enter the directory first.
When Active Directory was built, that meant a human manually added it. “Machines” were physical servers that got delivered to the office, installed in the server dungeon room, and registered by a human admin.
Human approval doesn’t scale to developers creating and deprecating testing databases, Kubernetes clusters, and CI runners at will. Contemporary AD implementations deal with this by deferring authority. An admin token (sometimes hardcoded…) automatically joins new identities.
Using human credentials to join new machines is a workaround that negates the point: Admin approval implies a human can tell you about each trusted device.
No admin can know every EC2 instance, PostgreSQL database, or CI runner in the organization. This is also because when AD was built, machine identities were long-lived devices, not ephemeral cloud resources.
Active Directory was built for human approval of long-lived infrastructure, but now often auto-approves short-lived cloud resources.
Even if you built all of the complex automations to reflect every testing database and Kubernetes pod in AD with automated admin approval, it’s security theater. The unified directory would exist on paper, but lack authority.
Modern cloud infrastructure automatically asserts machine identity:
- In Kubernetes, each pod gets a service account token, which allows it to assert its identity within the cluster.
- In Azure, you can configure a machine identity in Entra ID and let Azure’s Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) automatically issue OAuth tokens when machines request them.
These two examples have modern assumptions baked in: machines need to self-serve their identities when they’re spun up. They also assume a narrow scope.
Scope: how identity perimeters have changed
The unified directory of identity management aimed to encompass every device, user, and piece of infrastructure. Authenticating to the Domain Controller would be enough to get access to everything a user/machine needs and nothing they don’t.
This is the identity perimeter: where an identity is valid. In the Active Directory era, the perimeter was as large as possible. The more complete the perimeter, the more authoritative the directory. As an example, SQL Server accepts Windows authentication (i.e. an AD identity) or SQL authentication (username and password). Active Directory admins choose Windows auth to keep the perimeter large.
Anything outside of the directory would be a “shadow identity”: a valid identity that grants access to corporate infrastructure, but isn’t accounted for in identity management (unless you consider the post-it note on my monitor identity management).
A separate username-password set creates a separate perimeter. This used to be a problem, but is now the norm. Each API key, database string, or auth token creates a separate perimeter because they’re a credential that represents an identity for just one service. As an example, GitHub automation requires personal access tokens or GitHub private keys and doesn’t work with any directory identity.
But just to make it harder, zero-trust architecture makes machines constantly authenticate to each other, which skyrockets the count of credentials and creates hundreds of perimeters.
In theory, a small perimeter shrinks the blast radius of any breach: A compromised Notion session token should only give Notion access. In practice, an attacker may find additional credentials in Notion, which lets them expand their access. Oh, and the physical security layer of firewalls and physical perimeters is gone in the cloud era, so a leaked credential works from any attacker’s laptop.
This should concern admins more than it does: many teams keep troves of sensitive plaintext credentials in .env files or hardcode them in configuration files. The response is often lackluster:
- Use SSO where it’s available for human users
- Teach the team how to securely handle plaintext machine credentials
A solution like Active Directory is nearly useless for solving these issues.
The new paradigm
Organizations can tame the complexity of machine identity in the cloud, but not as simply as one massive Active Directory list. Instead, we see two main vectors to fix this:
The first is identity federation, where one platform trusts another platform’s approval to authenticate a workload. All three major clouds support this.
Using OpenID Connect (OIDC), AWS can sign a token for an EC2 instance to access PostgreSQL in Azure. Entra federated credentials natively support this use case and would trust the EC2 workload.
This works for many use cases. If you’re exclusively on AWS and run Terraform from GitHub Actions, OIDC federation straight into IAM does the job: You get visibility, know why you trust it, and know its scope. But it’s laborious to implement each relationship, which means it relies on IAM administrators who can barely keep up with group membership requests. Moreover, if said pipeline is breached by, say, a supply chain attack (which are common nowadays), the whole perimeter is breached.
Even if your admins are bored, no cloud has native bridges between every possible tool, so federation stops as soon as any service only accepts an API key. Organizations shouldn’t accept unruly, long-standing plaintext credentials outside of security purview.
That’s why organizations adopt a brokering approach. Here, credentials live in a secrets manager like Infisical (which securely stores and then delivers secrets to workloads at runtime). This creates a meta-perimeter for all of those micro-perimeters. Infisical (or another tool) acts like a broker: Machines authenticate to it, they broker access to the credential store, and inject the credentials the identity can read into its runtime.
These two patterns can bring order to the Wild West of machine identity in the cloud era. They check the boxes Active Directory once did:
- What identities exist? You have an overview of who authenticates and what they do
- What vouched for the identity? You know where workloads originate and why they’re trusted without relying on a human to approve everything
- Where is the identity valid? Keys, tokens, and strings have a natural perimeter.
This is especially important as organizations increasingly adopt AI agents, which often need their own identities, separate security policies, and even separate security tooling. Getting machine identity right is more important than ever. If you can’t keep track of testing databases and a Stripe API key, you don’t want autonomous software that can create its own databases and send that API key to strangers online.

articles.title: The Nvidia scandal isn’t slowing down
articles.body:
For years, Jensen Huang has had an almost unprecedented power to shape AI’s advancement as Nvidia’s CEO, cofounder, and president. As The Verge wrote last week, Nvidia’s chips are “the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built.” Ever-increasing demand has consistently outpaced supply, leading AI CEOs to essentially bow at Huang’s feet as they vie for more compute ahead of their much-hyped IPOs. Nvidia also has a varied investment portfolio of up-and-coming AI companies from neoclouds to infrastructure firms, worth nearly $100 billion, and Huang has President Donald Trump’s ear. He’s even been called Trump’s “most influential adviser” when it comes to technology. As of last Wednesday, however, Huang — a pivotal figure in the industry — is no longer CEO of Nvidia.
The Nvidia scandal isn’t slowing down
Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.
The Nvidia scandal isn’t slowing down
Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.
Since Huang’s resignation last week, the scandal over his multiple affairs has shown no sign of waning. After the announcement, Nvidia shares dropped 14 percent, making it one of the worst weeks on the market for the company in the past year and a half. And the revelations kept coming. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had had a third affair with a second employee (though the employee was unnamed). We learned that Huang had reportedly misled Nvidia leaders about his infidelity, that Nvidia was allegedly linked to the supply of nearly $12 billion of its chips to China, and that alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang’s companies reportedly promised advanced chips to Chinese AI company DeepSeek.
There’s reportedly been a petition to bring back Huang by some Nvidia employees, as well as reports of Huang assembling a “war room” of allies to float a comeback as Nvidia CEO. Lawmakers have begun investigations into the alleged chip-smuggling and other offenses. Every day, there’s increasing evidence of fallout inside the Trump administration. And as Nvidia’s quarterly earnings on Tuesday loom, the future of the company and the AI industry as a whole remain in flux.
What does an Nvidia without Huang look like? It’s hard to say, since he’s been at the helm for 33 years. CFO Colette Kress has taken on the role of interim CEO, and the broader AI world is waiting to see where one of the world’s most valuable companies — and one that helped shape the industry’s every milestone — goes from here.
Nvidia is such a large company that the implications of Huang’s departure “will take years to play out,” says Stephen Straus, CEO of KUNGFU.AI, an AI consulting firm. “[Nvidia has] their market share … they have the world’s best chips, they have the most manufacturing capacity … and they have a whole ecosystem built around what they’ve done. None of that changes with one person.” While there’s been discussion of Huang’s departure speeding along an AI bubble burst, Straus compares the situation to the dot-com bust — which didn’t stop the growth of the internet itself.
Huang’s resignation may not cause a domino effect in AI, but longer-term AI funding initiatives championed by him may eventually be affected, says Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm. Huang championed fundraising for the broader AI buildout: In August, Nvidia signed deals with six large financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund AI infrastructure expansion, and those agreements or future ones could look different if “the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals,” wrote Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello in a note last week on Monday.
Some lawmakers were already planning to pull CEOs before Congress
Far downstream of the biggest companies, smaller AI startups are wondering how the effects will trickle down. Michal Miernowski, co-founder and CEO of Amperos Health, which builds AI agents for healthcare billing, sits in the applied AI space about two layers removed from Nvidia. He doesn’t anticipate Amperos being directly affected much by the moves, since it relies on a mix of frontier AI models and open-source ones, but a cooling of the larger AI market — whether due to the Nvidia scandal or broader concerns — could stall business as well. There’s also more to come on Nvidia’s side, from the company’s investigation into Huang’s actions to congressional inquiries. Evan Gotlob, partner at DarrowEverett LLP and a former state and federal prosecutor, said he thinks “there’s definitely more” to the story about potential leaks to China and suspicious chip dealing. He added the board’s investigation would “obviously” continue despite his departure: “The investigation is really not going to turn out anything good for him.”
Some new lawmakers already planned to haul CEOs to Capitol Hill to testify under oath. The AI populism movement is growing, as well as the blowback against data centers, which was a key talking point in Democrats’ campaigns during the midterms. The revelations around Huang, a major Trump ally, provide an early opportunity to take action.
“We want to see a Democratic Congress investigate Nvidia for anti-competitive practices that pass off costs to consumers, what the company knew about chip smuggling operations with China, and what Nvidia received in exchange for donations to the Trump campaign and ballroom,” Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, told The Verge.
AI safety researchers also worry that in the worst-case scenario, the instability around last week’s events could speed up potentially dangerous AI milestones like recursive self-improvement, i.e., powerful AI that can autonomously improve and build future versions of itself. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, an AI safety firm and third-party auditor, said he worries that the volatility stemming from Huang’s departure “actually increases loss of control risk because companies feel even more revenue pressure and therefore are more willing to cut corners on safety.”
Early last week, before Huang’s resignation, the general consensus among Silicon Valley heavyweights, analysts, and politicians was that Huang’s “irreplaceable” impact would mean a return to the status quo for Nvidia. Colello wrote in a note that day that the firm “can’t rule out … Nvidia returning to business as usual” since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” Now, as Huang reportedly assembles allies to push for a comeback the likes of which haven’t been seen since the 2023 Sam Altman coup, the entire AI industry is waiting to see which way it will go.

articles.title: Should Jensen Huang Return as Nvidia's CEO? Supporters and Critics Disagree
articles.body:
Should Jensen Huang Return as Nvidia's CEO? Supporters and Critics Disagree (theverge.com) 83
			
		 	
				"Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive," reports Reuters, "and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter."
One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House...
The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang.  
The Guardian adds that Friday two major Nvidia shareholders "urged the board to keep 'all options' open."
In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look "outside" the company for its next chief. "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said on Fox News.  Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang's affair with the alleged spy for Beijing... Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang's behaviour within the next 10 days.   
The Guardian also notes Elon Musk "and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company... "
The letter demands that the company's board members "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts"...  Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang's return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco's most renowned business incubator.  Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had "erred, yes — to err is to be human — but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company". More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company's workforce.  
But it's difficult to verify the authenticity of signatories, notes The Verge:
  Business Insider reports that signatures include "Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor" and "Xi Jingping," likely a misspelling of Chinese president Xi Jinping.
Not all believe Jensen Huang should be allowed to return to his seat. According to the Financial Times, one ally acknowledged that, "Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense."  23andMe founder Anne Wojcicki told Bloomberg that "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible ... We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Wojcicki endured a messy public divorce from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, after it was revealed he was having an affair with an employee.

articles.title: I posted in "Who wants to be hired?" and a recruiter sent me a RAT and a stealer
articles.body:
A Recruiter Sent Me a Take-Home Test. It Takes Its Orders From an Ethereum Wallet.
A fake recruiter, a VS Code extension that shows one script and runs another, and malware that looks up its server in Ethereum transactions. Read without running a line of it.
On 10 November a recruiter emailed me about a DevOps Engineer role. The email came to the alias from my post in the October “Who wants to be hired?” thread on Hacker News and named two companies from my CV. The next step was a coding assessment inside VS Code, through an extension from the official Marketplace.
I didn’t install it. I downloaded the package, read it, and followed every address it pointed to. At the end of the trail there is a remote-access tool and a credential stealer. The part I enjoyed is in the middle: the malware finds its server by reading the latest transaction of an Ethereum wallet. That wallet is public, so four months of the operator’s server moves, working hours and money are public too.
The email
The message itself was fine: the right role, real employers (both are on my public profile). The problems were one layer down. The sender’s domain, huntrole.org, was registered seven days earlier, the DKIM signature didn’t verify, and iCloud had already filed the message as spam. And the assessment could only be done in an extension that starts together with the editor.
The careers site won’t take an application without a PDF resume, so it collects CVs even from people who never open VS Code. I sent it an invented candidate and got a ticket ID and instructions pointing at the extension.
The extension shows one script and runs another
There is no malware in the package, and that’s the design. On every editor start the extension (huntrole.assessment-tool, 126 installs on 16 November) sends the hostname and VS Code’s machineId to api.huntrole.com and keeps a WebSocket open.
When the assessment panel opens, the server returns a task with two code fields. The panel “types” displayScript on screen, then passes script to new Function with the real require and process: files, network, child processes. No ticket and no Run button needed.
For a device the server didn’t know, script was 150 harmless bytes. After my invented device registered and opened the socket it was 8,665 bytes, and displayScript hadn’t changed. So a scanner sees a clean package, and so does a candidate who reads the files before installing.
The server address is a transaction
The long script has no server address in it. It has a wallet address and code that looks up the wallet’s latest transaction. With the names cleaned up:
const wallet = "0x1eEf0849EDa15d87f64e51C73C8442Cf3c8bCEF3".toLowerCase();
function decode(to) {
  const bytes = Buffer.from(to.replace(/^0x/i, ""), "hex");
  const ip = (b) => b[0] + "." + b[1] + "." + b[2] + "." + b[3];
  return [ip(bytes.subarray(0, 4)), ip(bytes.subarray(4, 8))];
}
to is the recipient of that transaction. An Ethereum address is 20 bytes, and the operator fills them with an IPv4 address, the same address again, and 12 bytes that spell helloipbot!!. The transaction moves zero ETH and nobody owns the recipient.
From here on, that recipient is a marker, a transaction to it is a ping, and the sender is a pointer wallet.
The script doesn’t search for the ping. It rounds the current block number down to a multiple of 1,000 and opens six blocks around the round numbers, so the writer has to be punctual. If those are empty it falls back to a block explorer, and nothing checks the record’s age, so a wallet that has stopped writing still points at its last server.
For the operator this is cheap and hard to take down: no registrar can remove the pointer, and a ping costs about 0.00007 ETH. In exchange, every server they ever used, and the minute they switched to it, stays on a public ledger for good.
Three wallets, eleven servers
Every marker ends in the same 12 bytes, so the wallets can be found from the other side. I scanned every Ethereum transaction since 1 April for that ending and got three senders. Between them: 1,157 pings to 11 servers from July to 15 November.
- The early wallet worked for three weeks in July and starts with a developer’s test transactions: the text hello as data, markers that decode to addresses no packet can reach. I couldn’t find it in any public report.
- The second ran from 25 July to 19 October, with 607 pings to eight servers. It’s the wallet from the August reports on trojanised npm packages.
- The third is the one in my script: 303 pings to five servers since 4 September. It last switched on 12 November, two days after the email.
Nine of the eleven servers, and api.huntrole.com too, sit at one hosting company, Evoxt. The two newest are at another, Virtuo, side by side in one /24.
The timer counts blocks
The typical gap between pings is 200.6 minutes, which is exactly 1,000 blocks. Of the third wallet’s 303 pings, 270 landed in a block whose number ends in 999, 000 or 001, the blocks the script opens first. The timer keeps a fresh copy of the record where the reader will look, even when the address hasn’t changed.
The treasury that pays for this keeps hours. Its key has signed 284 transactions on 14 chains over 37 days, none of them between 12:00 and 22:59 UTC. The email’s Date header says +0500, and on that clock the signing hours look like a working day. Both are trivial to fake, so I won’t name a time zone.
Where the gas money comes from
The pointer wallets have burned about 0.08 ETH in four months. One treasury wallet funded two of the three, and each of its three top-ups was followed by a server change: 7 minutes, 8 minutes and 44 hours later.
The treasury’s own money looks stolen, though the ledger alone can’t prove it. On 3 September nine wallets, idle for months and mostly tied to each other by old transfers, sent it what they held within half an hour, on Ethereum and several other chains. The treasury sold the tokens, bridged about 12,560 USDC to BNB Chain and cashed out through one-time addresses of what looks like a swap service. Nine days later someone, I think the owner, moved what was left to a fresh address, and none of it went to the treasury.
It happened again on 3 November. A private wallet sent the treasury 5,344 USDT on BNB Chain and a little ETH on Ethereum within four minutes, and about twenty minutes later the treasury swapped it and moved it on.
Wallet files are on the stealer’s list, but nothing on chain says it emptied these wallets. Their addresses stay out of this post.
The treasury also pays people: 32 USDT transfers to eight addresses since September, 3,813 USDT in total, at most 21% of what those addresses received this year. Two of the eight cash out through an address that forwards everything to a wallet the block explorer labels OKX, and two more into one labelled Lemon Cash. Both exchanges verify their customers. If the labels are right, someone with the authority to ask can get names.
Going in, there is no such door: two of the pointer wallets got their first ETH from FixedFloat, an exchange that asks for no identity.
The same wallets feed npm and PyPI
The recruiter front is one delivery channel of several. The second wallet’s address is quoted in at least 40 advisories in the OpenSSF malicious-packages repository, nearly all for npm. On 9 November JFrog described another fake recruiting company, AccuraSoftHire, whose take-home project reads the same wallet through the same paths with the same XOR keys. And the October reports on hijacked npm packages from GitGuardian, OX Security and Sonatype name the third wallet, the one in my script.
What arrives on the machine
I fetched each stage once from a disposable VM and decoded it without executing anything: two small loaders, a remote-access tool, a 1.4 MB injector that plants code into other applications, and a Python stealer.
The remote-access tool is byte-identical to a published DEV#POPPER sample. It dials out, so a home router doesn’t stop it, and it accepts arbitrary shell commands. The stealer copies browser databases, keychain files and wallet files. Since I ran nothing, I can’t say what it actually gets from a real machine. The injector I mostly couldn’t read.
Who is behind it
Vendor reports on related incidents attribute this family (PolinRider, DEV#POPPER) to North Korean groups. My data ties HuntRole to the family through identical bytes, shared wallets and shared servers. It says nothing about the country.
Is this the crew that took about 6.3 billion dollars from Binance on 29 October? By Binance’s account that attack also went through a fake hiring process with a coding assignment. None of the 453 addresses around this ledger is among the 608 Ethereum addresses in the FBI alert, and Binance has published no hashes or servers to compare. I found no link and can’t rule one out.
If you installed it
Check for the extension and for what the remote-access tool leaves behind:
code --list-extensions | grep -i huntrolels -la ~/.node_modules/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i npm-wsfind ~ /Applications \( -name "*.inz.cjs" -o -name "*.inz.orig" -o -name "*.inz.tmp" \) 2>/dev/null
- Installed, panel never opened. The server has your hostname and machine ID. As far as the code shows, nothing else ran. The extension can open the panel on its own, though, so if in doubt count it as opened.
- Panel opened. Assume the script ran, whatever the checks show.
- Any of those files exist. The machine is compromised. From another device, rotate everything your account could read: .env files, browser passwords and sessions, Git and cloud credentials, wallet seeds. Then reinstall Node and the patched applications, or rebuild the machine.
When Microsoft removes a malicious extension, VS Code uninstalls it automatically (so its documentation says). Whatever the tool planted stays.
Who has been told
On 15 November I reported the extension to Microsoft, the domains and mailbox to Namecheap, the careers site to Vercel, and the servers to Evoxt and Virtuo. Two hours later I had automatic acknowledgements. A day later the extension is still listed.
The operator was busy that day too. Five hours before my reports the treasury signed 29 transactions on ten chains, most of them moving its leftovers to an address it had never used. The next morning that address signed for the first time: it swapped some BNB into USDT and sent 60 USDT to one of the eight addresses the old treasury had been paying. It pays the same people, so I’m calling it the new treasury.
How I read it without running it
Coding agents did most of the reading, and a sample can talk to the model that reads it: a planted AGENTS.md is a prompt injection attempt. So the sample was only ever data, the model reading it had no network, no shell and no secrets, and anything dynamic ran in a disposable microVM with the network closed by default.
Indicators
Wallets, markers, servers, paths and hashes

articles.title: Nvidia was in trouble before the Jensen Huang mess
articles.body:
Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.
But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.
“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.
Already, competitors have started to move in.
Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.
Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.
Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.
Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.
And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.
Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.
In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.
China Challenge
While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.
Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.
Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.
Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.
Trend Spotting
Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.
Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.
Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.
But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.
But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.
Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.
Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.
Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.
“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

articles.title: Skydio's asymmetrical F10 Lightrunner solves a problem with fixed-wing drones
articles.body:
Skydio’s drones have always been magical. From MIT research and early prototypes to what I would argue is still the most advanced consumer drone ever made, this is a company that makes very cool stuff. Sadly, Skydio no longer makes cool stuff for consumers, instead focusing on drone platforms for public safety, inspection, and other things that, on a good day, don’t affect me personally.
Even so, a new drone from Skydio is worth paying attention to, especially when it’s as weird as this one—the F10 Lightrunner is a fixed-wing camera drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight, all while looking so lopsided that it’s surprising that it can actually fly.
The benefits of asymmetrical aircraft
There’s a short rabbit hole you can go down if you start looking for other examples of asymmetrical aircraft. In the 1990s, legendary aircraft designer Burt Rutan and his company Scaled Composites built some decidedly odd airplanes, including the Model 202 Boomerang. But perhaps the most famous asymmetrical aircraft was the Blohm & Voss BV 141, a World War II-era reconnaissance plane that featured an engine in the middle alongside a crew compartment alarmingly offset out onto the right wing. The unique design was intended to give the crew the best possible view for reconnaissance missions, because in a typical single-engine aircraft, the crew sits right behind the engine, limiting forward visibility.
Nearly 90 years later, the Skydio F10 is applying a similar philosophy to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, which typically track targets by flying around them in circles. “While turning at low altitudes, it becomes very hard to avoid occluding a camera with a wing or a tail,” explains Andrew Goessling, director of engineering at Skydio. “So we were analyzing a lot of these use cases, and one of our engineers just blurted out, ‘What if we put the camera on the wingtip?’ And that’s where it all started, because as long as you only turn left, a lot of these problems just go away.”
Of course, putting the camera on the F10’s wingtip creates a bunch of new problems, chief among them that the aircraft is no longer balanced. Not only is the camera payload fairly heavy relative to the total mass of the drone, but its bulk also creates greater drag. This is why the seemingly straightforward solution of putting something else (like a battery) on the other wingtip to rebalance the drone isn’t practical, says Goessling. “The issue there is that the camera represents a substantial portion of the total aircraft drag, so putting something else on the other wing would cut your flight time nearly in half.”
The F10’s wing-mounted camera payload necessitated asymmetrical wings and uneven motor placement.Skydio
Goessling points out that there’s nothing inherently bad about an asymmetric design like the F10; it just makes the life of engineers either a little more difficult or a little more exciting, depending on your perspective. “There were really two challenges here: What is the optimal design for an aircraft with a wingtip camera, and then once you have the design, how are you going to control it?”
Any fixed-wing aircraft design has to consider three factors: distribution of mass, how thrust is distributed between the motors, and how the shape and location of the wings affect the aircraft’s aerodynamics. Once Skydio decided on their requirements for the F10—including the wingtip camera, two motors to enable controllable hovering for takeoff and landing, and a high top speed and long flight time—the engineers used a modeling-and-optimization approach to explore design options. The resulting aircraft compensates for the wing-mounted camera payload by extending just that wing to provide more lift on that side, and repositioning the motors asymmetrically to balance thrust against the added drag of the camera.
Maneuvering with MegaDock
The MegaDock can autonomously launch, recover, and recharge up to five F10 drones using a robot arm to grab them out of the air.Skydio
An added challenge was getting the F10 to launch and recover with a robot arm, using a storage, charging, and deployment system called the MegaDock. That requires the drone to transition from hover to forward flight and then back again—a particularly difficult trick for a flying wing with no tail control surfaces (movable parts of the wing used to steer the aircraft). The F10 uses model predictive control (a control technique based on a detailed physics model of the robot) to accomplish this autonomously, and a single control policy can handle the robot all the way through its entire flight envelope, from a stationary hover to its maximum flight speed of 100 miles per hour. In other words, there’s no “hover mode” or “flight mode,” so the mission planner just tells the drone where it needs to be, and the drone will know how to get itself there.
In operation, Skydio’s MegaDock can handle up to five F10s, allowing for continuous flight operations with three drones while two recharge. The entire system is fully autonomous, with humans only needed for remote supervisory control, communicating with the F10 via dual 5G cellular modems. Maximum flight time is 2 hours, and the aircraft is equipped with the same kind of magical obstacle-dodging camera setup as Skydio’s quadrotor drones. If something goes seriously wrong, an integrated parachute in the F10’s butt will deploy, lowering the drone to the ground gently enough to safely fly over people.
Goessling is the first to acknowledge that the F10 Lightrunner is an unconventional design, but he’s proud of what he and his team have come up with as a commercially viable solution to the occlusion issue with other fixed-wing drones. “It looks weird, and we got some pushback from some of the less technical parts of the company,” Goessling says. “If there were less crazy ways of doing it, we would have pursued them. But we have the data. We have sound reasons for every decision we’ve made. And the outcome at the end was well worth it.”

- Skydio Demonstrates Incredible Obstacle-Dodging Full Autonomy With New R1 Consumer Drone ›
- Skydio 2 Review: This Is the Drone You Want to Fly ›
Evan Ackerman is a senior editor at IEEE Spectrum. Since 2007, he has written over 6,000 articles on robotics and technology. He has a degree in Martian geology and is excellent at playing bagpipes.
