articles.title: First phase of embedded assessments at OpenAI
articles.body:
Our first phase of embedded assessments
We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.
Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.
Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems(opens in a new window) with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.
In this pilot assessment, Apollo Research(opens in a new window) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:
- Training did not incentivize subversion.
- Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.
- Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.
- Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.
For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.
Goodfire(opens in a new window) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.
We intend to conduct two assessments with METR(opens in a new window), focused on model alignment and monitoring:
- Alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.
- Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment(opens in a new window) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.
Transluce(opens in a new window) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.
OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.
We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.
Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.
Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.
Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.
Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.
Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests, and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.
Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.
Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.
These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.
We’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.
In the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

articles.title: Generative AI Usage in the Games Industry
articles.body:
The following manifesto was written by members of the IWGB Game Workers' Branch in collaboration with members of Game Workers Unite Ireland of the Republic of Ireland, CSVI of Spain, and the FIOM-CGIL Milan Work Council
Introduction
Our Aims
We, a collective of video game unions and work councils from Europe, write this manifesto to raise awareness of the harms of generative AI (genAI) use within the video game development sector.
GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce. Left unchecked, this harm will continue to grow and impact more workers, more games, and more players, even more acutely.
Our goal is to bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce, as well as to set guidelines and standards for games industry workers, stakeholders, and regulators, suggesting actions which can be taken to reduce – and ideally eliminate – these dangers.
Scope
This manifesto discusses genAI in the context of the video game development sector. These uses include, but are not limited to:
- The creation of assets included in a released game which are experienced by players – for example: art, sound, code, and dialogue assets.
- The creation of materials which are used as part of the process of development but which players won’t experience when playing the released game – for example: early concept art, reference materials, pre-translations, etc.
By “genAI” we mean a specific type of AI used to generate text, pictures, videos, or music in response to limited inputs (usually just text “prompts”) using LLMs and other energy-intensive models. The wider harms of genAI won't be covered here, but they constitute additional extremely compelling reasons to resist the use of genAI. These include:
- Severe harm to the environment (Zewe, 2025)
- The destruction of communities (Nguyen, 2025)
- The exploitation of the Global South (F.Regilme, 2025)
This document won’t go into detail about how different genAI models work, nor discuss the comparative quality of their output.
The focus of this document is on games industry workers (us!), how we are and will be impacted, and how we can resist.
The Impact of GenAI
GenAI Creates Worse Working Conditions
- GenAI is both directly and indirectly replacing game industry workers.
- Many game workers are being forced to use genAI, either explicitly or implicitly.
- Working with genAI is less desirable, fulfilling, and educational than the same work without genAI.
- Over time, working with genAI leads to worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout.
- Using genAI removes a sense of ownership from workers.
- GenAI is causing a marked decline in junior positions within the industry, leading to a lack of new talent.
Proponents of generative AI claim that it is a tool of empowerment for workers. For that to be true, every worker would be free to choose if, when, and how to use it. We would also need to trust that every employer would use the promised productivity improvements to benefit their workers.
In practice, this is not what we are seeing.
In many workplaces today, workers are being forced to use genAI ‘tools’, sometimes in very specific ways (Plunkett, 2025). Some companies do not explicitly impose the usage of genAI, but set expectations which cannot be reached with or without its use. Allowing the choice of usage, while also creating expectations that the worker should be able to keep pace with automated procedures, is no choice at all (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025).
When workers do use genAI, they find work more onerous than before. Many of the tasks related to genAI work are more tedious and less fulfilling, since the work becomes less about exercising the skills workers have built and invested in, and instead pivots to a plethora of small, parallel tasks which amount to supervising genAI and bug-fixing its output.
Workers using genAI have reported ‘AI brain fry’ and reduced focus (Pearl et al., 2025). Although gains to productivity are possible, these tend to be short term. Employees often initially work faster, take on larger tasks, work overtime, and ignore breaks, due to working with genAI feeling 'more like chatting' (Rangantathan & Ye, 2026). However, once this novelty declines, so does productivity, with workers reporting cognitive fatigue, burnout, and inhibited decision making.
A recent study (Shaw & Nave, 2026) showed that participants who used genAI frequently adopted results that were systematically incorrect, especially under time pressure but also in the face of incentives and feedback. The researchers were able to prove that users of genAI habitually delegate their agency and offload decision making to an external party with relative ease. They call this process ‘cognitive surrender’ (Shaw & Nave, 2026).
The use of genAI also removes a sense of ownership from workers, who become alienated from the results of their labour: the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers’ stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them.
GenAI is disproportionately used for work which would traditionally be given to junior workers, and is hence directly reducing the amount of junior positions available within the industry. This is worsening an already existing problem for newcomers to the industry, who are finding it harder than ever to find work, but it is also a loss of potential fresh perspectives, and is staggeringly short-sighted when it comes to the industry’s sustainable future.
GenAI has a profound negative impact on workers by reducing the availability and appeal of work. Games are best made by people, and people do their best when they are healthy and connected to their work, refining their skills and accumulating real experience.
GenAI Harms Relations Between Workers and Employers
- GenAI is sold to employers as an alternative to workers.
- GenAI often increases pressure on workers when used by employers to set policy, timescales, etc.
- GenAI can be used by employers to abdicate responsibility.
GenAI’s promise to employers is to more fully automate processes, to enable them to be completed with fewer workers. This directly reduces the amount of jobs available for game workers. In some cases, workers have even been forced to train the models which then replaced them, leaving them unemployed.
GenAI interfaces are engineered to be human-like and eager-to-please, to prioritise keeping the user engaged, even if engagement comes at the cost of providing them with incorrect information. GenAI’s predisposition towards this sycophancy and lack of real-world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions (Cheng et al., 2026).
In addition, when employers engage with human-like genAI models which never tell them ‘no’, they become less receptive to criticism and pushback from other workers.
GenAI can also obfuscate and confuse employers’ accountability, in two main ways. Firstly, employers may shift their own accountability onto these platforms, blaming an error on the “tool”, rather than accepting responsibility themselves. Secondly, they may blame workers for issues which arise through the use of genAI – which the employers have mandated.
Any time genAI is used without exacting human verification, the possibility of error increases. Exacting human verification takes time, which negates the promise of genAI automation, and therefore many employers are choosing to skip this step, either directly or indirectly by imposing time constraints on workers which make detailed verification impossible. Workers are then blamed for failures in the genAI’s output.
Employers see genAI as a way of cutting labour costs, employing fewer workers than they would need to without it. GenAI companies ingratiate themselves with employers, by promising the impossible. Moreover, mistakes made by genAI are often blamed on the workers, rather than the employers mandating its use.
GenAI Appropriates the Work of Workers
- GenAI models are often trained on stolen third-party data, with employers failing to credit or compensate the original creators.
- Where genAI models are trained on internal data, employees/creators are likewise rarely credited or compensated.
GenAI models are mostly trained on stolen datasets, and, as stated by the owner of a genAI company, ‘impossible to create’ without stealing data (Milmo, 2024). Employers often feel entitled to automatically include their employees’ contribution into their internal dataset without consent and/or extra compensation.
This point does not require much explanation, but please do not let the relative smallness of this section undermine its importance: stealing the creations of others is wrong, creating very similar versions of those creations is wrong, and using those similar versions to generate wealth which the original creator does not share in is wrong.
GenAI does not create, it appropriates. Content output by genAI has its origins in the work of humans, who are rarely compensated for that output.
GenAI Perpetuates Discrimination
- Most genAI models are trained on datasets that carry an intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities.
- GenAI content averages out data used to train the AI, leading to a homogenisation of culture.
GenAI models are trained on vast swathes of historical data which is often unvetted and without context, as they aggregate large amounts of data and look for commonalities to generate a response without any direct connection to reality. The use of old data can reflect outdated opinions and values which we would be horrified at today, as well as generate middle of the road solutions.
The predominance and absence of certain types of people in historical data can also reinforce their predominance or absence in the output of genAI models today: for example, the predominance of white male doctors in historical medical literature may lead genAI models to assume that a referenced doctor is white, or to create a white male character when asked to create a doctor.
Within the games industry, this has two main types of effect: it can increase discrimination within workplaces, for example, when used in hiring practices, and it can reduce the range of representation within created media, leading to more homogenous characters and viewpoints in the games we create and play.
GenAI reproduces both historical and contemporary biases and can lead to both implicit and explicit discrimination, including but not limited to racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, etc.
GenAI Has Hidden Costs
- GenAI’s output is unreliable and often incorrect.
- GenAI providers obfuscate the cost of genAI, its inner workings, and its limitations.
- GenAI providers aim to silo and monopolise knowledge to sell it back to corporations.
GenAI providers obscure a significant portion of their associated costs (to the environment, mental health, etc.), which impacts the ability of workers to make an informed choice on whether and how to use them (Nguyen, 2025).
GenAI platforms also disincentivise education on their limitations. Average usage of genAI goes down with increased understanding of how genAI actually works behind the scenes (Tully et al., 2025, 20).
GenAI providers sell employers a seductive image of the future, where production can be fully automated. However, in actuality, genAI platforms are gatekeeping transferable skills (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025). Once a model is trained, the ‘owner’ (usually a large conglomerate) of the trained AI has a uniquely powerful position and complete ownership over skills that were previously owned and shared by workers.
This is bad for workers, but it is also bad for employers who outsource their knowledge and skills to third-party genAI providers, as once these companies have a monopoly on this previously institutional knowledge, their prices are unlikely to remain competitive.
GenAI providers aim to replace employers’ dependence on workers with dependence on their own models. Companies which buy into this promise while genAI usage is cheap may come to regret this when it is the only option and prices increase. Workers will regret this much sooner.
Recommendations
Given the present and future impact of genAI on the games industry, we make the following recommendations:
Recommendations for Workers
We understand that the industry is very unstable at present, and that can make it more difficult to speak out. Please do as much as you are comfortable with, and remember that we are stronger together.
- Avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible.
- Make your voices heard.
  - Distance yourself from genAI usage.
  - When genAI content is presented to you, question its use and express dissatisfaction.
  - Talk to your colleagues about the risks and harms of genAI.
  - Make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI.
  - Support other colleagues when they speak out about genAI.
- Do not burn yourself out because of artificially inflated expectations. Do not be a hero by trying to work at an unrealistic pace.
- Educate yourself on how to spot genAI content so that you can avoid accidentally using it in your own work.
- Seek out information on your company’s genAI services from impartial sources, and share it with your colleagues.
- Ask your local worker representatives to negotiate an agreement on genAI usage for your company. Discuss its contents with your colleagues.
  - This agreement could reinforce protections on refusing to use genAI.
  - You could ask to form a committee to evaluate/investigate violations on genAI usage.
- Organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat.
Recommendations for Employers:
- Listen to your workers.
  - Involve the workforce in development of policy regarding genAI.
  - Workers should be the ones who decide when, where, and how to use it.
- Listen to your customers.
- Avoid the use of generative AI entirely.
  - Ensure that no worker is required to use genAI.
  - Disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development and prototyping.
  - If it is absolutely impossible to avoid usage, label/declare usage precisely.
- The chain of accountability at work should be respected and managers should be held accountable for the output of their team.
- Inform workers about the negative outcomes of using genAI. Information should come from impartial sources, not companies trying to sell their genAI services.
- Schedule training for workers on how genAI actually works behind the scenes, its real limits and capabilities.
- Do not use your employees’ work as training data. If you do:
  - Only use data after explicit consent.
  - Ensure fair compensation for reuse of their labor.
  - Allow them to withdraw their work from such datasets.
Recommendations for Players:
- Support games made without genAI.
- Be vocal about disliking genAI in games – leave comments, make videos, ask for change.
- Educate yourself on how to spot genAI content so that you can avoid it.
Recommendations for Regulators:
The UTAW Tech Workers’ Inquiry have put together an incredible resource with suggestions for regulators which we wholeheartedly agree with:
https://techworkersinquiry.org/ai/
In addition to their points, we would also like to suggest that:
- It should be forbidden to submit a person’s work to any genAI dataset without explicit permission and consent, and most importantly without fair compensation for reuse of labour.
- Any acceptable submission must be for datasets that are transparent in how data is used, stored, and retained. Workers must be able to withdraw their content from such datasets at any time
Conclusion – GenAI Against Humanity
GenAI is worsening our working conditions. Our belief is that workers should be the ones who decide when, where and how to use it, as they are the ones who know how to do their jobs. No one likes being forced to do something that harms them, and a lot of workers are being forced to use genAI against their will.
We do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games;
it is not inevitable.
If genAI was just a useful tool, as advertised, it would make our lives easier and we would have more free time, but the opposite is happening. The owners of these tools are aware of this and that is why they push it: to normalise it, to spread its use, and to ensure it becomes indispensable before raising prices. They are the ones in power, not workers, not even CEOs in video game studios.
We firmly believe that video games are nothing without the humans who make them – they are a way for us to express ourselves, to share knowledge or a point of view with the world, to entertain all kinds of gamers. There is no intent in anything made by a genAI probabilistic engine. If no one put their skill, effort, soul, and time into making a game, why would anyone waste their time playing it?
In the current context, everything has to be data-driven: percentages, averages, time spent, productivity… But quality is subjective and cannot be measured, so companies disregard it. People want high-quality games, they want to spend their time playing a game whose developers poured everything into making it, because they are more enjoyable, as it happens with any other art form.
Years after the public release of genAI chatbots, their use has not been as widespread as their owners would like, but they have been deployed as an excuse for mass layoffs with the goal of pleasing shareholders. We should stop thinking about what is good for business, but instead think about what is good for society in general, for workers, for gamers. What good is it if a CEO earns millions every month if the working conditions at their studio are worsening, along with the video games they create?
No genAI will be able to replace the humanity in any work of art.
We are sick of shareholder value being the be-all and end-all of this industry.
We are sick of watching five giant conglomerates just shuffling money around in a giant scam to be the winner of this never-ending hype contest.
We are sick of seeing people fired or forced to quit just to maximise profits.
We are sick of being told to just accept that this is what is good for business.
GenAI is bad for workers and games. Workers, protect your interests. No games get made without our collective strength. Organise. Fight for your rights.
FAQ
- What happens if most of my colleagues want to use genAI in some capacity? In other words, if a developer really wants to use genAI as part of their process, can they use it?
- The short answer is yes. Obviously the other problems are still there, therefore you should decide as a collective if you want to use it, on the whole, given concerns around the environment, cost, ethics, law, honesty, the sanctity of art, etc. Our aim in this document is to educate people about the harms of genAI, so that both employees and employers are less inclined to use it.
- What if the quality of the output is good, or good enough?
- This doesn’t change the main focus of our manifesto. We want workers’ conditions to improve, and to organise against abuses and for better ownership.
- Why are you talking about AI and not layoffs, RTO mandates, workplace toxicity, etc.?
- While the issues caused by genAI are coming from the same place as these other adjacent crises, the genAI situation is developing rapidly and has practical knock-ons to every aspect of our industry. We’re still working on the other issues plaguing our industry, with old and new methods, and we encourage everyone to join us in that fight.
- How do I know if I should get compensation for an AI-generated output? Is there even a way to find out if a specific data entry was important for a generated output? Or to remove a data entry from a set?
- There are examples of research going in this direction like “WAGLE: Strategic Weight Attribution for Effective and Modular Unlearning in Large Language Models” (J Jia, J Liu, Y Zhang, P Ram, N Baracaldo, S Liu, 2024) and “Losing is for Cherishing: Data Valuation Based on Machine Unlearning and Shapley Value” (Ma, Le ; Yang, Shirao ; Wang, Zihao ; Wang, Yinggui ; Wang, Lei ; Wei, Tao ; Zhang, Kejun, 2025), but the specific implementation is not important.
- Why are you against the future?
- We are not. We simply believe that workers have the right to shape their future. Being exploited and overworked is not a future we are willing to accept. Time will prove genAI ‘tools’ and their usefulness, let us not be trampled in the meantime. The future is not yet written.

articles.title: The Secret ThinkPad Powerbutton Code to Bring Dead Laptops Back to Life (2007)
articles.body:
The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life
Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.
Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.
So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.
I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”
And so it is.
So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.
Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This little code is now the coolest “cheat” code I know…

I think 2Smart is right. It’s not entirely uncommon for one to have to press the power button once or twice with no power attached to release the residual charge built up in capacitors. When the unit attempts to start it will use up the remaining power in the unsuccessful attempt. From there, you can sometimes start the machine. A common manifestation of this problem is fans spinning but no display. This can manifest after a power outage or other unexpected shut down.
It sounds to me like this particular system board has issues discharging properly.

1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default.
Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery.
I hope this helps

articles.title: The Secret ThinkPad Powerbutton Code to Bring Dead Laptops Back to Life (2007)
articles.body:
The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life
Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.
Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.
So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.
I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”
And so it is.
So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.
Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This little code is now the coolest “cheat” code I know…

1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default.
Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery.
I hope this helps

articles.title: FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours'
articles.body:
FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours' (techcrunch.com) 6
			
		 	
				The FBI is warning (PDF) that hackers are using the AI-powered penetration-testing tool Artex to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers and Barracuda. TechCrunch reports:  Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim's network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. [...] After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool's developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains "widely accessible" for use in cyberattacks.
It's not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration -- including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
articles.body:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.
Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.
The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.
Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.
A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
Updated with response from Barracuda.

articles.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
articles.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

articles.title: New James Bond Announced and the Name's Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
articles.body:
Robert Pattinson has been announced as the successor to Daniel Craig, becoming the seventh actor to play the role in an official Bond movie.
The news was revealed on the official James Bond social media accounts account on Monday. All earlier content was abruptly wiped from 007 on X and Instagram just before 3pm GMT and a repeating message typed out: “Identity confirmed.”
The film studio then released a first photo of the actor in Bond’s trademark tuxedo with a press release confirming the news and saying Pattinson’s casting will “usher in a new era for one of cinema’s most celebrated characters”.
In a statement Pattinson said: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime … To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”
The announcement came after a drawn-out casting process, in which Pattinson was understood to be on a five-strong shortlist, which included Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. On Friday suggestions emerged that Pattinson had been offered more favourable contract terms than his rivals, fuelling rumours that he was the strong favourite for the role.
Craig’s final film as Bond was No Time to Die, released in 2021 after being delayed due to the Covid pandemic. The narrative for the 25th film in the series lent the franchise a sense of closure, with Bond apparently dying before a title card promised: “James Bond will return”.
Craig made five Bond films in total, starting with Casino Royale in 2006. During his tenure the franchise became a box-office record-breaker, with 2012’s Skyfall alone taking $1.1bn globally.
Pattinson, 40, is due to appear in the next Bond film, the 26th in the franchise (although two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983, take the total to 28). The as yet untitled project will the first to be shot since Amazon-MGM Studios purchased the rights to the series for more than $1bn in 2025 from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, heirs to original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.
Harry Potter producer David Heyman and Spider-Man producer Amy Pascal will oversee the franchise, while the Dune trilogy’s Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight is writing the script.
Pattinson has demonstrated his versatility across a wide variety of roles, earning a reputation as an actor with broad enough appeal to support major blockbuster films while retaining artistic credibility with offbeat and unlikely choices. He first came to notice in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and achieved superstardom opposite Kristen Stewart as vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight film series. He appeared in films directed by David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis, Maps to the Stars), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse) and Lynne Ramsay (Die My Love), and returned to franchise film-making with The Batman in 2022.
The first actor to play Bond on the big screen was Edinburgh-born Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No. So successful was the film that Connery returned to make four further films over the next five years, which are considered by many to be some of the franchise’s finest: From Russia With Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball and You Only Live Twice. Bond creator Ian Fleming’s preference for the role, the English actor David Niven, starred in the non-canonical Casino Royale (1967), while the Australian model George Lazenby joined for one outing, 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, before Connery rejoined for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).
Roger Moore then lent the series a more ironic spin for his seven films between 1973 and 1985, which include The Spy Who Loved Me, Moonraker and Octopussy. The role then went to British actor Timothy Dalton for two films in the late 1980s; a six-year gap preceded Irish actor Pierce Brosnan’s debut in 1995 in GoldenEye. He shot four films as 007 before Craig’s tenure began.
The official James Bond films have so far made a total of $7.8bn, making the franchise the fifth highest-grossing in history. Proceeds from merchandise and sponsorship deals are estimated to far exceed that figure.
Catherine Shoard will be in the comments from 5.30pm today to answer readers’ questions about the casting.

articles.title: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
articles.body:
A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.
This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft.
Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.
“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.
“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”
With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.
“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.
What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.
Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.
The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.
Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.
Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.
The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.
The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.
