articles.title: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
articles.body:
Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

articles.title: OpenAI: Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse
articles.body:
Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support
New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
Today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.
It is well(opens in a new window) established(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.
Helping more organizations detect abusive material
We’re building on our current protections with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.
Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)(opens in a new window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.
We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.
Child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition(opens in a new window) and ROOST(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.
We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.
Results
Early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:
- The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.
- Images flagged by the new classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.
Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal(opens in a new window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.
More information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card(opens in a new window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.
Interrupting harmful behavior and pointing people toward help
We already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.
The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.
We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children(opens in a new window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.
Practical support for developers
The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance(opens in a new window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition(opens in a new window), Thorn(opens in a new window), NCMEC(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.
The guidance provides clear rules, ways for users to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier, Moderation API(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer(opens in a new window).
Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.
We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.
Supporting child-safety law enforcement units
Protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.
We’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with new tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.
The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.
Continuing the work together
These efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

In fal(opens in a new window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.
More information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card(opens in a new window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.
Interrupting harmful behavior and pointing people toward help
We already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.
The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.
We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children(opens in a new window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.
Practical support for developers
The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance(opens in a new window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition(opens in a new window), Thorn(opens in a new window), NCMEC(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.
The guidance provides clear rules, ways for users to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier, Moderation API(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer(opens in a new window).
Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.
We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.
Supporting child-safety law enforcement units
Protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.
We’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with new tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.
The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.
Continuing the work together
These efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

articles.title: Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing
articles.body:
Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing (propublica.org) 66
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied ProPublica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. "Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back."

articles.title: How Billions in Safe Insurance Money Is Being Bet on A.I. Debt
articles.body:
Supported by
How Billions in Safe Insurance Money Is Being Bet on A.I. Debt
Insurance companies are investing billions of their customers’ money into A.I. deals as analysts warn of mounting risks.
When Elon Musk needed help financing a large purchase of artificial intelligence chips earlier this year, Wall Street offered an elegant solution.
Mr. Musk and his team of advisers created a financial entity that would borrow billions to buy the chips and then lease them back to xAI, his artificial intelligence effort. This way, xAI wasn’t technically the borrower, which helped make its official debt load look smaller to investors.
To help fund this complicated arrangement, $2.4 billion of the debt was sold to an insurance company called Athene, which manages life insurance policies and annuities for retirees, according to a Moody’s Ratings report.
The deal was part of an increasingly popular playbook: tapping insurance companies, which are historically among the most cautious investors, to make loans to tech titans like Mr. Musk and further fuel the A.I. boom.
The amount of A.I. debt being held by insurance companies has soared this year. U.S. life insurers, including some of the largest like Athene and Corebridge Financial, held $85.2 billion in A.I. debt as of June 30, up 24 percent from six months prior, according to Moody’s.
While this accounts for just 2.1 percent of life insurers’ total debt, their exposure is expected to grow quickly. Life insurers could hold up to $185 billion of A.I. investments by the end of next year, according to Moody’s.

articles.title: Doing Show HN generates a ton of automated email pitches
articles.body:
Show HN -> a ton of automated email pitches
I posted Airdash on Show HN last week. Over the next four days, 17 services wrote to the Airdash inbox to sell me something, and nearly all of them were written by software that read my HN title and nothing else.
Let's go through it.
Seven of the 17 are launch boards and directories: AI tool lists, "Product of the Week" battles, a 3D city map of SaaS products. The hook is usually a dofollow backlink, the price somewhere between free and $49. The other ten sell security scans, competitor reports, agent testing, demo videos, Reddit promotion, newsletter sponsorships, distribution to other people's coding agents, and one wants an affiliate deal.
"SQLite databases for agents with an Airtable view" shows up in almost every email, reworded just enough to look like someone read it. One directory pasted my whole Show HN title in as the product name, so it would love to feature "I built SQLite databases for your agents with an Airtable view for you."
"No follow-ups, promise." "This is the only email you'll get about it." "Not a mailing list, just a one-time note." One of them then sent me the same pitch three times.
Here they are in order of arrival, Madrid time. I replaced the names of the services and the people with [brackets] and took out the links, to protect the innocent.
1. Friday 16:20, a security scanner

Thanks for building,

giving agents real sqlite databases with an airtable view people can actually read is such a clean idea. day one launches usually get one spike and then go quiet. want me to list airdash on [Service] so agent builders keep finding it after today, yes or no?

I run [Service] and have a labelled sponsor seat open. First month free, then $29/mo, locked 6 months, month to month.

[link]

[Name]

articles.title: Dffy: A fast terminal-native Git diff viewer, written in Rust
articles.body:
A terminal diff viewer for git, written in Rust.
Built for large repositories, up to the size of the Linux kernel.
dffy                   # everything you haven't committed
dffy main..HEAD        # any revision git understandsbrew install --cask amalucelli/tap/dffy
# or
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amalucelli/dffy/main/install.sh | sh
# plus the experimental renderers: … | sh -s -- --plugin markdown --plugin mermaid
Then try it in any repository: dffy HEAD~10.
dffy is a diff viewer for the terminal. Run it in a git repository and it opens a full-screen view of your changes: a file tree on the left, the diff on the right, split or unified. Pipe it, and it prints the diff instead.
It's built for big diffs. Instead of computing the whole diff up front, dffy shows the first files as soon as it finds them and works on the rest in the background, so a 13,000-file change opens as fast as a one-line fix.
It fits into how you already work. Every action is a single key, the layout adapts from a wide monitor down to a phone over SSH, and dffy can stand in for git's pager, git add -p filter and difftool. Settings live in a plain config file you can keep with your dotfiles.
dffy builds on tools I like: the terminal review flow of lumen, the review UX of hunk, and the rendering of diffs.com (Pierre's @pierre/diffs). None of them fit how I work. lumen centers on AI features I didn't want in a diff viewer. hunk is TypeScript on a JavaScript runtime, and I wanted a single native binary that stays fast on huge repos. diffs.com runs in the browser. So I built a native terminal diff viewer that works the same on a laptop and over SSH from a phone.
Fast
- ⚡ Opens the Linux v6.0..v6.1 diff in 9.5ms and loads the rest in the background.
- 👀 --watch repaints as you edit, stage and commit.
Reading diffs
- 🪟 Split or unified, picked by terminal width.
- 🌈 Syntax highlighting for 30 languages, with changed words emphasized.
- 🌳 A syntax-aware diff (d) that marks reformatted (~) and moved (») code.
- 🔁 Renames detected the way git detects them.
Navigation
- 🗂️ A file tree, a fuzzy file picker and search across the diff.
- 🎯 Each file opens at its first change, and n/N jump between changes.
- ⌨️ Single-key actions, with a command panel on space.
Git
- 🧾 Staged, unstaged and untracked changes in one view, or any revision.
- ⚔️ Conflicted files from a merge, rebase or cherry-pick, with their conflict markers highlighted.
- 📟 Works as git's pager, git add -p filter and difftool.
- 📁 Compares files and folders outside a repository too.
Anywhere
- 📱 Works on phones over SSH, with plain-letter keys and a frameless layout.
- 🖱️ Mouse selection that copies over SSH.
- 🎨 16 themes and a config file for your dotfiles.
- 🧩 Renderer plugins (experimental): Markdown diffed as rendered text, and Mermaid flowcharts and sequence diagrams drawn in the terminal.
Scripts and agents
- 🧱 --json: the diff as JSON Lines, with each line's kind and whether it moved or was only reformatted.
- 🤖 dffy mcp: an MCP server that lets coding agents list a change's files and read its diffs a page at a time.
dffy                        # staged, unstaged and untracked changes
dffy --staged               # what's staged (git diff --cached)
dffy HEAD~3                 # a revision against the working tree
dffy main...feature         # changes since the merge base
dffy show HEAD              # a commit with its message
dffy main.. -- src/         # limited to paths
dffy a.txt b.txt            # two files or folders, no repository needed
dffy --watch                # refresh on every change
dffy --syntax v6.0 v6.1     # diff by syntax
dffy --stat main..          # also --name-only, --name-status, --exit-code
dffy --json main..          # JSON Lines for scripts and agents
dffy mcp                    # an MCP server for coding agents
With git:
git config --global core.pager dffy
git config --global interactive.diffFilter "dffy --color-only"
In the viewer, n/N move between changes, f/F between files, / searches, o finds a file, space lists commands and q quits. ~/.config/dffy/config holds key = value lines; dffy config --default lists every key with its default.
🟡 means partial support. All seven are open source. GNU diff is GPL-3.0-or-later and the rest are MIT. Checked against hunk 0.25.0, lumen 2.32.0, difftastic 0.72.0, delta 0.20.1, diff-so-fancy 1.4.14 and GNU diffutils 3.10, with a source for every cell.
Opening Linux v6.0..v6.1 (13,168 changed files, a 48MB patch) in a viewer, time until the first changed line is on screen:
As git's pager, dffy streams the whole 48MB patch in 3.0MB of its own memory, about as fast as plain git diff.
dffy is written in Rust.
- 📚 A library at its core, dffy-core: the diff model the viewer, printed output, JSON and the MCP server all share.
- 🧮 Its own diff engine: histogram and syntax-aware diffs, renames matching git's.
- 🖼️ Its own terminal renderer, with no TUI framework. A full frame takes about 200µs.
- 🌊 Streamed input and output, so the first screen doesn't wait for the whole diff.
- 🛰️ One shared watcher per repository, however many views are open.
The documentation covers every key, flag and setting: installation, usage, the viewer, keys, configuration, themes, git integration, watch mode, renderer plugins, JSON output, the MCP server, troubleshooting, architecture and benchmarks.
MIT

Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC. A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.”
Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
Nvidia’s board of directors is still focused on an investigation into Huang, CNBC reports.
Since Huang’s resignation last week, tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures, including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues.
Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct.

articles.title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
articles.body:
Less than a week after an issue with air traffic control communications and radar caused the FAA to halt takeoffs nationwide, United Airlines departing flights are being disrupted by an outage. The airline has said it is working to get things up and running again as quickly as possible, but without much detail about the issue itself.
United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
Is everything down right now?
Is everything down right now?
The outage is also coming after last week’s global Microsoft Outlook shutdown, and the great-bank-outage-that-wasn’t earlier Monday afternoon. According to posts on social media, a number of people onboard the planes have heard from their pilots that a systemwide IT outage for United has caused problems with a weight and balance calculator that has stopped them from getting clearance to take off.
United tweeted that “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.” So far, there’s no word on when it expects the problem to be resolved, and when the impacted flights will be able to leave for their destinations.

articles.title: Tell HN: HN is being scraped for emails to scam
articles.body:
I know that many folks here post their personal emails in the Who's for Hire monthly pages and other places, and want to remind you that this public site gets views from folks with ill intent (or their bots/agents) as well. I use unique emails for every site, so I immediately knew that the late AWS payments email sent to my HN email were fake. There were other tells, but I want to remind everyone to be vigilant! HN is public but even social media sites where you supposedly can make your page private I've had some of those emails suddenly have spam sent to as well. Please be safe everyone!
My favorite tells that an email is a scam:
- Before opening a surprising/suspicious email, hover over the sender name to see the domain the sender came from (don't open the email if it's strange).
- _If_ you already opened the email, before clicking any links in the email, hover over them to see the domain that the link sends you to.
There are dozens more tips but a full article would be required, and these two will prevent you from falling for nearly all of them.

articles.title: AI-Generated Books Confront Publishing Industry With Big Questions
articles.body:
AI-Generated Books Confront Publishing Industry With Big Questions (theguardian.com) 87
			
		 	
				Romance novelist Coral Hart publishes her own romance novels for the Kindle, and found a kind of superpowere when she realized "the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month," reports The Guardian:
 Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself "high six figures".  Like any Kindle Unlimited author, she is only paid per pages read: it would make no business sense for her to churn out books that readers quickly abandon...   "So, it's not taking the human out of the equation. It's taking the friction and the time and the business blocks out of the way."
One study (awaiting peer review), led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates that around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. Hart now teaches courses on how to use AI to produce books. Unless disclosing the use of AI becomes a legal requirement, she advises other authors not to do so because of the public response.   "The minute someone discloses [AI use] they get death threats, they get called names, they're ousted," she says.... In the literary world, many people fear the tech will undercut and replace them. "I think people are very afraid of AI, and people in publishing are delusional in thinking that it's not going to overtake our industry, that their screaming on social media is going to stop it." 
But the anger comes from another place, too. If large language models can spit out books that people want to read, or produce a convincing pastiche of your favourite writer, that's almost certainly because they were trained on established writers' stolen work....  Many writers oppose AI for both moral and aesthetic reasons. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers — Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan — to promise that they will "never release books that were created by a machine". The publishers did not promise.  [Tess Callero, a literary agent with Europa Content, says] "...you have to wonder the reason they aren't. Is it because they see a future in which potentially these books could be monetised?"] 
So where do we go from here? Will big name writers win the argument for keeping AI out of literature, or will our bookshelves and e-readers soon be crammed full of AI-generated stories? And if a reader can't distinguish human from machine writing, does it still matter? 
The Guardian's author notes this new technology brings new challenges to the book publishing world:
-  Publishers have concerns about US copyright law, "which specifies that a book must be 'human authored' and considers AI-generated text public domain. "
- The article notes high-profile books being canceled after accusations their writers used AI.  But even in those cases, "Another unresolved question is if and when publishers should withdraw books," since if publishers liked it enough to make the deal, shouldn't they stand behind that judgment?
-  And should there be a way for authors who want to experiment with AI to work with top book publishers?  (One theory is publishing houses are afraid of alienating a handful of top writers who almost universally oppose AI.)
"Right now, to write without the aid of a machine is to swim against a strong cultural tide," concludes the article's author, noting a recurring reaction from friends who "have looked at me with something close to pity when I tell them I would never use AI to write."

articles.title: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
articles.body:
Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson Is Officially James Bond
articles.body:
It’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson.
The “Batman” and “Odyssey” star has officially been cast as the next James Bond, ending months of rabid speculation about which young actor Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve would hand the keys to the Aston Martin.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Added Villeneuve, who recently directed Pattinson in the upcoming “Dune: Part Three”: “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”
Amy Pascal, who has produced the “Spider-Man” franchise and several 007 films, and David Heyman, behind the “Harry Potter” series, are producing the new Bond film, with Tanya Lapointe executive producing. Steven Knight is writing the screenplay.
Pattinson picks up the 007 mantle after Daniel Craig’s five-movie run as the womanizing super spy, which began in 2006 with “Casino Royale.” Craig’s final turn was in 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which ends with Bond sacrificing himself to save the world from a secret global terrorist organization. “No Time to Die” was also the last film in the series released before longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM for $20 million.
Predictions about who would be the next James Bond had taken over media and the industry in the last month, and a shortlist of British actors took turns as the presumed favorite. Jacob Elordi was pegged for the role in the earliest days of swirling rumors, but reports since surfaced that the “Euphoria” star didn’t even screen test for the part. Jack Lowden seemed like another safe bet. In early September, his “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman claimed Bond was already picked and cheekily added that his “fingers are crossed” for Lowden. However, Lowden’s run at the character was largely overshadowed by Callum Turner, who seemed like a sure pick until news of Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult’s auditions was revealed. At that point, it became anyone’s guess who would come out on top until Pattinson was ultimately chosen. Other actors in the mix included Josh O’Connor, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles.
It’s not hard to see from Amazon MGM’s perspective why Pattinson was the obvious choice. He is, almost unquestionably, 2026’s most in-demand movie star and has the box office record to show for it. With help from Zendaya, Pattinson drove A24’s “The Drama,” an intimate yet squirmy original dramedy, to $134 million worldwide from a budget of $28 million. “Primetime,” in which Pattinson starred as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, likewise hit big with $61 million globally against a slim $18 million budget. Pattinson also starred as the sniveling Antinous in “The Odyssey,” which did $1.8 billion, and is set to star in “Dune: Part Three” in December, which is sure to pull in the big bucks. (It’s very possible Pattinson earned the part after impressing Villeneuve on Arrakis).
Pattinson also has the big IP experience needed to lead a franchise like James Bond. In 2022, Pattinson debuted as the titular Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman.” He is set to revisit Gotham for the sequel in 2028. Those doubting Pattinson would land 007 often pointed to his obligations to Bruce Wayne as a reason why he could never take on Bond. However, after several production delays with “The Batman Part II,” it seems Pattinson is ready for a new longterm relationship with another familiar big-screen icon.
“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” said producers Pascal and Heyman. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

articles.title: Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains
articles.body:
Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains
By Krisy Gashler
Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds.
A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters.
“Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”
For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%.
“We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said Steve Grodsky, paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”
Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. articles.title: It's always DNS, so why are we running our own?
articles.body:
This will be a rollercoaster story on how we ended up replacing Route53 and running our own authoritative DNS server.
Before our lives changed
At some point, we decided we should be able to provide unlimited basins to our clients. Basins are a core namespace construct on S2 and act as top-level containers for streams (already unlimited in number). We found that customers were hacking around our not-so-arbitrary limit of 100 basins per account. That’s not a cool experience.
For the purposes of this story, what is important is that each basin created by a customer becomes its own subdomain: my-basin.b.s2.dev (not different from the way buckets work on AWS S3). The DNS entry associated with each basin is a CNAME, which routes clients to the correct cell in our architecture. To support unlimited basins, we'd therefore need to support unlimited DNS records.
These records would need strong consistency too. When a basin is created, its address should be instantly resolvable, otherwise clients would be waiting around for a cached NXDOMAIN to expire.
My pulse went through the roof at the thought of running our own DNS server, yikes!
Hooking on existing systems
My research phase started with hope. Hope that our existing DNS setup with AWS Route53 would work with these new requirements. I really really did not want us to build and run our own DNS server.
Route53 is an awesome system and can, it appears, support an unlimited number of records. But, there's a fatal limitation: their API rate limits at a max of about 5 UPSERTs per second (AWS throttling docs have recently changed, the limits may be higher now).
This was something we discovered the hard way, actually. I did read the docs but the API limits didn’t raise any concerns. It became obvious when a nefarious actor rapidly created 10s of thousands of basins, saturating our entire quota of Route53 records. This generated a backlog of work that required a few hours to process, during which our normal DNS updates were stuck, with processes trying to delete records while others tried to add new records. It did make for a great post-incident review though. This was when we started enforcing the 100 basins per account limit.
We looked at the option of batching, but that would break our goal of making entries instantly available. And even with batching, the setup did not feel “unlimited”; it would still be possible for legitimate use of the system to hit the rate limit.
Other managed DNS providers we looked at (GCP Cloud DNS, Cloudflare, Azure DNS) have similar limitations: if you update/insert/upsert records using the provider API, there’s a heavy limiting component.
No way around it, a custom authoritative DNS server had to be built (double yikes!)
The new DNS system
The technical requirements were pretty straightforward: given any DNS request that comes in, we need to query an up-to-date zone map, which should be able to hold unlimited records, and send a corresponding response back to the client.
To avoid syncing to a separate system and having yet another moving piece, the DNS records would come directly from our existing basin database. A live SELECT would consistently “resolve” the required mapping in the DNS request. In other words, we wanted DNS to simply become a new caller of our existing, strongly consistent account database.
Our account database lives in Google’s Cloud Spanner where performance was expected to fare well (given enough money that is).
Next came the core functionality.
We went back and forth between building on a library or writing a CoreDNS module. A library ended up feeling like the most flexible path, which would allow us to build something very specific to our use case. We are a Rust shop, but we decided to go with Go for this project, mostly because the Spanner tooling (and the GCP ecosystem) is comparatively more mature. We quickly settled on the miekg/dns library due to its excellent doc quality and the many RFCs under its belt.
We needed to be able to support authoritative DNS queries for several types of records: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, SOA. Since we were using a library we had to build the responses ourselves. Our correctness testing focused on these, and consisted of unit tests, RFC compliance testing using Ferret (which we discovered in this great paper: SCALE: Automatically Finding RFC Compliance Bugs in DNS Nameservers) and a post-deploy smoke test with live data.
S2 uses wildcard certificates for the basin zone and they need ACME DNS-01 challenges to work. We decided not to serve the DNS challenge from our server and offloaded it to a separate Route53 zone using CNAME delegation, to avoid tweaking our cert renewal systems as well as serving dynamic TXT records.
We then went through a few planning sessions with a popular AI system. The design was simple enough, things made a lot of sense (even for me), except that the recommendations constantly included various extra features: coalescing, negative caching, throttling, rate limiting, DNS cookies, etc. Expected, for a system that would sit live on the open scary internet; however, it was a lot of suggested protection.
The more we pulled on this thread ... the scarier it got. There are many types of attacks that can happen at the DNS level, scary things I knew of and things I never heard of.
NXDOMAIN attack is the one that made us the most afraid. Every random non-existent DNS query would be a fresh database lookup. We tried building in-app defenses for NXDOMAIN however, it is, in my opinion, the worst DDoS attack and nothing can really stop it. Not cool.
The case for a DNS Firewall
Long story short, the possible attacks on DNS infrastructure scared me more than I would like to admit. We went looking for a DNS firewall solution. We were sure there must be something like a reverse proxy setup for DNS serving. Either this is a niche setup or it’s a very dangerous world, but for our requirements of unlimited records and DNS reverse-proxy firewall type, we found only two companies: Cloudflare and Akamai. Both giants in their own rights, both with similar offerings (it’s the kind that has no public pricing).
A few POCs later, we ended up picking Cloudflares DNS Firewall solution. Our DNS server origins were configured to only allow traffic from Cloudflare’s known IPs, a pretty standard reverse-CF setup (Cloudflare in front and nobody else gets to the origin, otherwise what’s the point). With this missing piece, we were now at our final design and ready to roll the new system into production.
As an authoritative DNS server, we have to reply to SOA and NS queries, and they point to nameserver IPs. We took extra care to ensure the IPs returned are always the Cloudflare IPs and not the load balancer ones, which included a ns-leak-test that ensures the origin IPs don't leak as part of some regression change.
Final architecture
For the final architecture and HA (yes, failures will always happen), we run the DNS server on two separate GKE clusters (in separate regions, choosing the closest possible to Spanner), each with multiple replicas behind a TCP and UDP load balancer.
Observability and training everyone on the new system were another key component of the rollout. While I don’t think anyone gives Route53 a second thought and I don’t think anyone monitors it separately (managed services are someone else’s pager after all), we had to create alerts and runbooks with late-night processes to recover from failures.
There is one funny part to this setup: explaining the full delegation chain. The main domain is managed by Cloudflare in a regular zone. Then it delegates the basin subdomain to Cloudflare, but not a zone, to a service (DNS Firewall). That service then connects to GKE. And there’s another zone in Route53 for the certs (good luck understanding that, Codex).
This isn’t even its final form, the internal TODO includes tuning DNS caching and how to properly optimize between clients/DNS Firewall/DNS app (no amount of AI can solve that), future DNSSEC extensions and many more. It is an unknown system when it comes to failures we don’t see (or the way I like to think about this, how do you know things fail when they look fine).
For now, things have been stable. Looking at stats for the past few weeks, live traffic looks good, the commit history for the past few weeks is mostly CVE fixes, dependency bumps and cost savings. Our customers now create thousands of basins, and they are instantly available for streaming.
I think we’re now in a place where we can blame DNS in one of our post-incident reviews.

articles.title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
articles.body:
At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded.
I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter.
Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek, founder of Matasano Security, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts:
Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative.
I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics.
Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t.
But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it.
First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head.
Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners.
Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company.
A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications.
When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer:
0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine.
1. Grab a copy of The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook.
2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2.
3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress.
If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive.
And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software.
To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job.
And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
articles.body:
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
