articles.title: The Delicious Limited-Edition California Olive Oil I’m Gifting Everyone This Year
articles.body:
The Delicious Limited-Edition California Olive Oil I’m Gifting Everyone This Year
I was binge-watching the latest season of Netflix’s Nobody Wants This, when I spotted a familiar bottle in the hand of Esther Roklov (played by Jackie Tohn). In the scene, the impeccably dressed potential future ex-sister-in-law (it’s complicated) brought Brightland’s Awake olive oil to a pivotal housewarming party. What a thoughtful gift, I thought to myself.
As fate (or manifestation) would have it, I learned that the women-owned brand was about to launch arguably its most festive (and giftable!) set yet. I got my hands on some bottles to give them a taste, and let’s just say I know what I’m getting a few people on my list this year.
Brightland’s New The Holiday Feast Set Is the Perfect Gift for Home Cooks
Inspired by the flavors of the season, The Holiday Feast Set contains a trio of consciously crafted olive oils and vinegar, plus two brushed gold stainless steel spouts for controlled pouring.
- Awake: The best-selling classic California olive oil in a limited-edition holiday design
- Feast: A California olive oil infused with sage, thyme, and parsley
- Velvet: A balsamic made with California Mission figs
The limited-edition set is typically sold for $120 and arrives in a beautiful holiday box that needs no extra wrapping. While this set isn’t included in the sale, you can use code KT for 25% off almost everything else on the site from November 16 through 18.
My Honest Review of Brightland’s The Holiday Feast Set
If you’re just hearing the hype, Awake is a bold, slightly peppery olive oil that — like the name suggests — makes your taste buds feel bright-eyed. It’s made with California olives that are cold-pressed within hours of harvest (so you know it’s fresh). It adds vibrancy to dressings, of course, and it’s a no-brainer for drizzling over soups, dips (especially hummus and labneh), meat, and really good frozen pizza.
Infused oils can be hit or miss, but Feast is a bullseye. Made with extra-virgin olive oil, sage, thyme, parsley, and nothing else, just a whiff evokes cozy cooking. It adds a deep herbaceous flavor to easy baked chicken thighs and roasted cauliflower and sweet potatoes, although I suspect its compatibility extends to all veg.
The Velvet fig balsamic vinegar contains just three ingredients: distilled vinegar, California Mission figs, and sugar. It’s not syrupy sweet, like some other bottles, but is fruit-forward with bright acidity and works equally well with both oils. (How about that?)
I paired it with Awake in a quinoa salad so good, I ate three times in a week. (I bought more arugula on Sunday to make it again — that’s how good it is.) I also combined it with Feast, for a restaurant-worthy bread dip.
As a set, this trio makes a statement. It’s stunning and thoughtful, which to me is the best kind of gift.
Buy: Brightland The Holiday Feast Set, $120 at Brightland
What’s your favorite gift to give home cooks? Tell us in the comments below.

articles.title: Rust changed me as a developer
articles.body:
How Rust Changed Me As A Developer
How Rust Changed Me As A Developer
The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1. That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did.
I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now. One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.
What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus.
Where were enums all my life?
We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:
struct Human {
    first_name: String,
    last_name: String,
}
The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each
other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first
names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to
speak.
But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3: the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants:
enum Person {
    Human { first_name: String, last_name: String },
    Cat { name: String, cuteness: Cuteness }
}
A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities.
Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type,
but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where
you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on
the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.
match some_person {
    Human { first_name, last_name } => { 
	    // do a thing with first_name and last_name
    },
    Cat { name, cuteness } => {
	   // do a thing with name and cutenes
    }
}
When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and
last_name. You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These
cases are distinct from each other.
It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People
using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model
optionality (null) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can
also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of
success), or an error (with a value describing the error).
Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.
Enums and abstraction
In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:
interface Person {
    def do_one_thing()
    def do_another_thing
}
class Human implements Person {
    ...
}
class Cat implements Person {
   ...
}
The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the
details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.
This is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface.
Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle.
But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.
Or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to
add Dog. Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles
Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to
see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going
to ensure you don't miss any spots!
Or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value.
In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile.
enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked.
Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction -
you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct.
Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox.
Dispatch galore
In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've
discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like
this:
if something {
   do_this_thing()
} else
   do_another()
}
Rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html].
There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled.
What if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties.
You could create an enum Person; either an enum or an interface with multiple
implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group
based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to
account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those
don't actually exist.
Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person
interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or
Cat) during compile time.
struct Group<T> {
   // some fields	
}
// compile time assembly, 
// then runtime creation of the assembled group of cats
let cat_group: Group<Cat> = Group::new();
Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.
In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is important.
Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.
Type driven development
When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4.
Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy.
Why create automated tests?
Obvious: Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working.
Subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.
Why write documentation?
Obvious: People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation.
Subtle: The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development.
Why write types?
Obvious: Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance!
Subtle: You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software.
This perhaps sounds like big design up front processes where people write all the tests, or all the docs, or all the types, in advance, and then do the implementation. 6 I'm not talking about this -- I'm talking about iterative development where you keep going back to tests, docs and types as you learn.
Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop.
Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development.
The Biggest Surprise
Here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros.
Let's talk about magic.
Say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle.
What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic!
Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort, runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust.
But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time.
With serde, Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this:
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Human {
    first_name: String,
    last_name: String
}
With clap, you create the type that
expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enums too!),
document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you
have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets
well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the
same type you used to express the CLI.
Like this:
/// My first CLI
#[derive(Parser)]
struct MyFirstCli {
    /// How many cats do you want?
    #[arg(long, short)]
    amount_of_cats: usize
}
Again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in
Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just said Rust
doesn't normally let you do that.
How does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code.
Code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too.
Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns.
Ownership and Architecture
Rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel.
Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box.
The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust:
class Item:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
      
class Container:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items
my_item = Item()
my_container = Container()
my_container.items.append(my_item)
my_item.value = "I change you!"
This also doesn't compile:
class Node:
   def __init__(self, parent, value):
       self.parent = parent
       self.value = value
       self.children = []
   def add_child(self, node):
       node.parent = self
       self.children.append(node)
Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference.
This feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it.
For circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas.
A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7.
Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner.
Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture.
The arena pattern everywhere
A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree, has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot.
The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference.
A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere.
In an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do?
- iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit.
- fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments.
- interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data.
- the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying.
Rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently.
Performance has a quality all its own
I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature
optimization? The
great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth,
argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for
writing efficient software.
Rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction.
When you have these tools available, need to develop new wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8. Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it.
But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9, it changes how you think. It changes what's possible.
Sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible.
But it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens. But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore.
While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis: a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar.

one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust
that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may
actually make your life easier -- enums, declarative type-driven frameworks,
and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not
that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and
learning new ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but
not always under the surface, there when you need it.
Rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10
AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code, then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more important to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave.
If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good.
You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like
true/false, or C's enum.
If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits?
Does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand? Natural language is inherently stretchable.
With AI we've seen the return of big design up front. I may be wrong, but I'm still skeptical of this approach, and still a fan of iterative development and incremental learning and theory building.
Not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do.
Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts...

articles.title: Rust changed me as a developer
articles.body:
How Rust Changed Me As A Developer
How Rust Changed Me As A Developer
The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1. That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did.
I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now. One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.
What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus.
Where were enums all my life?
We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:
struct Human {
    first_name: String,
    last_name: String,
}
The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each
other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first
names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to
speak.
But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3: the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants:
enum Person {
    Human { first_name: String, last_name: String },
    Cat { name: String, cuteness: Cuteness }
}
A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities.
Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type,
but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where
you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on
the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.
match some_person {
    Human { first_name, last_name } => { 
	    // do a thing with first_name and last_name
    },
    Cat { name, cuteness } => {
	   // do a thing with name and cutenes
    }
}
When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and
last_name. You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These
cases are distinct from each other.
It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People
using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model
optionality (null) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can
also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of
success), or an error (with a value describing the error).
Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.
Enums and abstraction
In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:
interface Person {
    def do_one_thing()
    def do_another_thing
}
class Human implements Person {
    ...
}
class Cat implements Person {
   ...
}
The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the
details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.
This is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface.
Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle.
But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.
Or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to
add Dog. Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles
Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to
see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going
to ensure you don't miss any spots!
Or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value.
In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile.
enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked.
Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction -
you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct.
Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox.
Dispatch galore
In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've
discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like
this:
if something {
   do_this_thing()
} else
   do_another()
}
Rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html].
There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled.
What if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties.
You could create an enum Person; either an enum or an interface with multiple
implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group
based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to
account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those
don't actually exist.
Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person
interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or
Cat) during compile time.
struct Group<T> {
   // some fields	
}
// compile time assembly, 
// then runtime creation of the assembled group of cats
let cat_group: Group<Cat> = Group::new();
Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.
In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.

When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. Subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]

articles.title: US Banks report outages in latest tech hiccup
articles.body:
Big bank customers report outages; JPMorgan Chase blames software bug with potential ripple effects
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Customers at banks including Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo said they experienced outages coast to coast on Monday — days after technical snafus wreaked havoc for flight passengers and Microsoft customers.
There were nearly 5,000 reports of outages at Chase and about 1,400 between BofA and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com.
JPMorgan Chase said a software bug in systems it runs in-house slowed service for some customers – and may have affected other banks.
“It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” JPMorgan said in a statement. It added that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds.”
The nation’s largest bank said other lenders may have been affected when JPMorgan was a party to a transaction with them, but that “this is not a systemic issue.”
In other words, reported outages at other banks appeared to be due to customers trying to do business with Chase accounts.
JPMorgan said it was working to resolve the problem by the end of the day.
Customers reported issues at Capital One, PNC, US Bank and the Zelle money transfer app.
Zelle indicated any problems customers faced sending payments were due to problems at partner banks.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should. Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds,” a Zelle spokesperson told The Post.
Capital One made a similar statement, suggesting it was indirectly affected by banking woes at Chase.
“Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” a Capital One spokesperson said.
Some customers said online they couldn’t use their banking apps.
“My Chase App has a warning that I’ve never seen before: Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later,” one user wrote on Reddit.
Earlier in the day, Chase said it was sorry to an X user complaining of banking woes.
“I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We’re sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience,” a Chase support account wrote on X.
The technical difficulties were the latest in a series of incidents to cause major inconvenience for Americans.
Air travel slammed to a halt on Friday, with authorities blaming a botched contractor job or a faulty router. After thousands of flights were cancelled through the weekend, some stranded travelers were still trying to make their way home on Monday.
Also last week, Microsoft had a widespread outage that prevented online communications for governments and companies for over 24 hours.
The software giant said Saturday services was fully operational for Teams, Outlook and other products.
Independent cybersecurity expert Katie Moussouris told the Post the extent of the bank problems suggested they were interconnected.
“It could be a really wild coincidence, but it seems like they share a component on the backend,” she said.
A former top Treasury Department official urged calm.
Ex-Assistant Treasury Secretary Graham Steele said things can get out of hand if people start to lose trust in the banking system.
“What really becomes a problem is when people don’t trust the banking system because they think it has become corrupted or compromised in some way,” he told The Post, adding that the Federal Reserve does worst-case-scenario drills to prepare for extended problems.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
articles.body:
Apple is working on a face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front-facing camera for authentication, and it’s already testing it with the new iOS 27.3 beta released today, as reported by MacRumors. Currently, the only way to unlock the iPhone Duo is by using Touch ID or entering a passcode, which might feel like a step back if you prefer face authentication using the Face ID feature available on other iPhones.
Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.
The iPhone Duo’s face unlock feature seemingly has a few caveats, however: it’s only available for the lock screen, you can only use your face for an unlock if you have used Touch ID or input a passcode within 45 minutes, and you can’t use the face authentication for Apple Pay purchases.
iOS 27.3 is set to launch publicly in December, Apple said last month, so should the feature make it to the full release, you may not have to wait too long for it to be officially available.
Apple reportedly wants to add Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo, Bloomberg reports.

articles.title: Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness
articles.body:
Some owners of Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display say they experience eye strain, headaches, and dizziness when using the laptop, with affected users pointing to the screen's brightness-control system as a possible explanation.
A significant number of complaints have appeared on Reddit, X, and the MacRumors forums since the new models launched earlier this month. The discussions on MacRumors include a dedicated PWM thread, a separate owner poll, and comments in the reviews and display-details threads.
On X, one user said trying the PROLED MacBook Pro in an Apple Store for around 30 minutes left them with a severe headache. The user said they had previously struggled with OLED screens before finding newer implementations tolerable, and called for an option to change the Mac's dimming behavior.
A Reddit user described how reading text, especially against a black background, brought on dizziness and nausea. They said their OLED iPad Pro did not produce the same symptoms. In the main MacRumors forum thread, a 16-inch PROLED owner reported a headache and mild nausea that began to ease after switching back to a mini-LED MacBook Pro. Another member, posting in the separate poll thread, said they were returning their PROLED laptop for similar reasons after previously having no difficulty with OLED devices.
The suspected issue is pulse width modulation (PWM). An OLED screen produces light through its individual pixels. With PWM dimming, the display changes the time spent at brighter and darker levels during a rapidly repeating cycle. Spending less time at the brighter level reduces the average amount of light reaching the viewer, making the screen look dimmer.
Those fluctuations can occur too quickly to look like an obvious flashing screen, but some people report discomfort with displays that use them. PWM frequency describes how often the brightness cycle repeats. It is different from refresh rate, which is how often the displayed image updates, so a 120Hz ProMotion specification does not tell you the screen's PWM frequency.
Notebookcheck's testing of the 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro recorded 240Hz flickering whenever brightness was set to 99% or lower, with a measured amplitude of 56%. In other words, the light output fluctuated 240 times per second, and the amplitude describes the size of those fluctuations. The publication warned that sensitive users could experience eye strain or headaches due to the specification.
Mini-LED MacBook Pro displays also use brightness modulation, but Notebookcheck measured a much higher frequency of 14,880Hz on the 14-inch M4 Pro model. Such rapid fluctuations are generally less likely to cause discomfort for PWM-sensitive users.
Apple already provides a Display Pulse Smoothing accessibility option on supported iPhones. The setting offers another way to dim the OLED screen at low brightness, although Apple cautions that it can affect display performance under some conditions. macOS does not offer an equivalent control, but Apple could add one in the future.
The OLED MacBook Pro models start at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch version. Apple continues to sell the mini-LED models alongside them.

articles.title: Show HN: CheeseDB – agent memory where deleting a source deletes what it taught
articles.body:
A database engine purpose-built for AI memory. Native Go · Provenance-aware · Revocable · Embedded
Every memory knows its sources. Ask it anything in plain English. Recall a bad source, and everything learned from it goes too.
An embedded, append-only, hash-chained memory database for AI agents, written in Go with the standard library only. Use it from Go, from the cheesedb command, or from Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP apps.
Website: cheesedb.dev
Status: preview. cheesedb is in active development. It has not yet had an independent security review, and the API and on-disk format may change before v1.0, so it is not yet recommended for production data. See Limits and the changelog.
An agent's memory is built from sources it cannot fully trust: user messages, web pages, documents, tool results. Sooner or later one of them turns out to be:
- wrong: a tool returned bad data;
- malicious: a web page planted instructions or false facts (prompt injection, memory poisoning);
- private: a user asks for their data to be deleted.
Deleting that source is not enough. Everything the agent learned from it stays in memory, and the agent keeps acting on it. A plain memory store cannot tell which memories came from where, so it cannot remove them. The demo shows this with a real LLM: after the bad source is deleted from a plain memory list, the model still gives the same wrong answer.
- Every memory records its sources. A memory is stored with the sources (or other memories) it was learned from. The engine refuses a memory without one.
- Recall removes exactly what depended on a source. One call removes the source and every memory built on it, however deep the chain goes. Memories that are still backed by another, independent source survive (Fair); or remove everything the source ever touched (Strict).
- Ask it in plain English. With an embedding model of your choice, cheesedb finds memories by meaning (search), answers questions from them (ask), and forgets what you describe after you confirm (forget). A recalled memory is never found again. Without a model, everything else works the same.
- Erase really erases. Recall(..., Erase) removes the text from the files on disk before it returns. cheesedb find searches the raw bytes to prove it.
- The history cannot be edited silently. Every record is chained by hash to the one before. Damage or edits are detected on every open, and erasing text keeps the chain verifiable.
- Agents are isolated by design. Each agent is reached only through its own token. No method takes another agent's name, so a prompt-injected tool holding one agent's handle has no way to reach another.
- Embedded and dependency-free. A Go library and a folder on disk: no server, no external dependencies.
You can model sources and memories in SQL, or as a graph in Neo4j. We did both, to compare: the same data on all four engines, with the same durability (every write flushed to the physical disk before it is acknowledged).
Benchmarks with 1M memories per agent, median of 3 runs, on an Apple M1 Max (macOS, internal SSD), SQLite 3.53, PostgreSQL 17 and Neo4j Community 2026.10. Full results, method and caveats: BENCHMARKS.md; the raw output of the run: bench/results/v0.3.0.
¹ A new connection to a server that is already running; booting the Neo4j server took 6.5 to 8.2 s in an earlier run. PostgreSQL and Neo4j ran over TCP on localhost, which adds a round trip to each statement. We wrote the Neo4j model and queries ourselves, and an expert may do better.
- Recall is where it wins. cheesedb keeps the dependency graph in memory and removes 10,000 memories with one write: about 13x faster than Neo4j, 45x faster than SQLite and 370x faster than PostgreSQL. The SQL versions run several statements for each affected memory. A graph database fits the job better, and Neo4j is the closest competitor, but it is still slower.
- The rules live in the engine, not in your code. No memory without a source, no memory built on a recalled source, recalls are permanent, agents cannot see each other. With SQL or a graph database you write and test these yourself.
- Erasure is built in. In a general database, a deleted row's bytes can stay in the files (free pages, the write-ahead log) until a vacuum or checkpoint. cheesedb's Erase rewrites the file without them before it returns.
- Writes are about even, because the disk flush dominates for every engine.
- You need SQL-style queries, filters or keyword search. cheesedb finds by id or by meaning. Keep other queries in your database, store only memory ids there, and check each result against cheesedb.
- Startup time matters with very long histories. cheesedb replays its log when it opens an agent: about 0.7 s at 1M memories. SQLite opens instantly. Snapshots are planned.
- An agent's memory does not fit in RAM. cheesedb keeps about 205 bytes per memory in memory, plus about 0.8 KB per searchable memory (768 values, one byte each).
- You need production guarantees today. cheesedb is a preview; see Limits.
go get github.com/govinargo-labs/cheesedb                          # the library
go install github.com/govinargo-labs/cheesedb/cmd/cheesedb@latest  # the command
Requires Go 1.26.5 or newer. Developed and tested on macOS; Linux runs the same tests in CI. Windows is not supported yet.
The peanut story, from the command line. A user is allergic to peanuts; a restaurant's web page says its satay sauce is peanut-free; the page turns out to be wrong.
cheesedb agent create story
cheesedb lot story user_message "I am allergic to peanuts"                           # lot 1
cheesedb lot story doctor_note "Allergy test result: peanut allergy confirmed"       # lot 2
cheesedb lot story web_page "Spice Garden menu: our satay sauce is peanut-free"      # lot 3
cheesedb remember story "The user is allergic to peanuts" 1 2                        # memory 4: from 1 OR 2
cheesedb remember story "Spice Garden's satay sauce has no peanuts" 3                # memory 5
cheesedb remember story "The satay at Spice Garden is safe for the user" 4,5         # memory 6: needs 4 AND 5
With an embedding model (setup), ask in your own words. Memories saved before the model was set up become searchable with cheesedb embed:
cheesedb embed story
cheesedb search story "can the user eat the satay at Spice Garden?"
# 6: The satay at Spice Garden is safe for the user (match 0.81)
# 5: Spice Garden's satay sauce has no peanuts (match 0.77)
# 4: The user is allergic to peanuts (match 0.57)
Without one, list what is alive: cheesedb active story.
Then the web page turns out to be wrong:
cheesedb recall story 3 fair erase        # recalled 3; memories removed: [5 6]
cheesedb search story "can the user eat the satay at Spice Garden?"
# 4: The user is allergic to peanuts (match 0.57)
cheesedb find story "peanut-free"         # not found anywhere (searched every file, byte by byte)
cheesedb recall story 1 fair erase        # memories removed: []: the doctor's note still backs the allergy
cheesedb verify story                     # OK. head fingerprint: ...
examples/plain-english runs this story step by step, with ask and a chat model, for a demo or a screen recording.
s, err := cheesedb.Open("/data/cheesedb")   // a folder you choose, created 0700
tok, err := s.CreateAgent("alice")        // returns Alice's token, once: keep it safe
alice, err := s.OpenAgent(tok)            // the only way to reach Alice's data
defer alice.Close()
a, _ := alice.AddLot("user_message", []byte("I live in Pune"))
b, _ := alice.AddLot("web_page", []byte("profile: lives in Pune"))
c, _ := alice.AddLot("weather_tool", []byte("Pune: rain"))
m1, _ := alice.Remember([]byte("user lives in Pune"), cheesedb.Leg{a}, cheesedb.Leg{b}) // learned from A, or from B
m2, _ := alice.Remember([]byte("Pune is rainy"), cheesedb.Leg{c})
m3, _ := alice.Remember([]byte("carry an umbrella"), cheesedb.Leg{m1, m2})            // needs M1 AND M2
removed, _ := alice.Recall(c, cheesedb.Fair, cheesedb.Untrusted) // the weather tool was wrong
// removed == [m2, m3]; m1 survives because it does not depend on C
cheesedb can find memories by meaning, so you and your AI can ask in your own words: "can the user eat the satay?" finds "the satay sauce has no peanuts". It needs an embedding model, which turns text into a list of numbers (a vector) so that texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. cheesedb stores the vectors, searches them, and removes them when their memory is recalled. The library never calls a model: the cheesedb command and its MCP server do, with the model you set up.
Set it up by adding an embedding model to ~/.cheesedb/llm.conf. Any OpenAI-compatible server works (Ollama, LM Studio, oMLX, vLLM, or a hosted API); a local one keeps your memories on your machine:
embed_base_url = http://localhost:11434/v1     # default: base_url
embed_model    = nomic-embed-text               # e.g. after: ollama pull nomic-embed-text
# embed_api_key = your-key                      (only if the server needs one)
If your chat server also serves the embedding model, embed_model alone is enough: the server and key are taken from base_url and api_key.
Use it:
cheesedb search alice "what should I eat?"    # the closest live memories, best first
cheesedb ask alice "what should I eat?"       # search, then the chat model answers from those memories only
cheesedb forget alice "the pizza place"       # shows the closest memory and what goes with it; erases after a yes
cheesedb embed alice                          # make memories saved before the model was set up searchable
cheesedb index alice                          # the agent's index and its model
Every memory saved with remember (in the command and in the MCP server) is made searchable at once, and MCP apps get a sixth tool, search. If the model is down, the memory is still saved and the answer says it is not searchable yet; cheesedb embed catches up. After changing the model, run cheesedb embed again: vectors of two models cannot be compared, so it rebuilds the index.
Without an embedding model, nothing changes: sources, memories, recall, erase, verify, reading by id, listing live memories and the five other MCP tools all work, and nothing is sent anywhere. If you already have a vector store, keep it, store only memory ids there, and check each result against cheesedb.
From Go, with vectors from any model:
alice.CreateIndex("default", 768, "nomic-embed-text") // dims and a label for the model
alice.Embed("default", m3, vec)                       // vec []float32 from your model
alice.EmbedBatch("default", items)                    // many at once, one disk sync per batch
hits, _ := alice.Search("default", queryVec, 5)       // []Hit{ID, Score}, best first
for _, h := range hits {
    it, _ := alice.Get(h.ID)                          // the text comes from the ledger
    fmt.Println(h.Score, string(it.Data))
}
ids, _ := alice.WouldRecall(m3, cheesedb.Fair)        // what a recall would remove, without removing it
- A recalled memory is never returned. Recall removes the vectors of everything it removes, at once. With Erase, the vectors are erased from disk together with the text, and both hash chains still verify (Verify, VerifyIndex). A vector can be turned back into an approximation of its text, so cheesedb treats it like the text.
- Exact search, small in RAM: the question is compared with every vector (cosine similarity), so there are no missed results and nothing to tune. In memory each vector takes one byte per value (about 0.8 KB at 768 values); the exact float32 values stay on disk, and the few rows that could still be in the top results are re-checked with them, so the answer is the same as a full float32 scan. The time grows with the number of memories; see How it scales.
- ask sends only what search found (10 memories by default) to the chat model, and tells it never to treat a missing memory as an answer, so it is told to say "I do not know" instead of guessing.
- forget finds memories, not sources. Sources are not in the search index; recall a source by its number. It shows everything that would go before it erases anything (WouldRecall).
- One index per model. Vectors from different models cannot be compared. From Go, to switch models, create a new index, embed into it, then DropIndex the old one.
- Without an index, nothing changes: same files, same head fingerprint, same speed. An index lives in its own folder with its own log (ARCHITECTURE.md section 9).
A Go program, offline with a stand-in embedder that matches shared words, or with a real model:
go run ./examples/vector-search
EMBED_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 EMBED_MODEL=nomic-embed-text go run ./examples/vector-search
cheesedb's own cost with a search index (768 values per memory), on an Apple M1 Max. No embedding model is included: with a local one, turning a question into a vector took 17 ms. Median of 3 runs; method and every number: BENCHMARKS.md.
The command and the MCP server open the store for every call, so each search reloads the index; they suit agents of up to about 100,000 memories. A Go program that keeps the store open loads it once. With real embeddings at 1M, search still ranked the right memories first among a million look-alikes, and none came back after their source was recalled.
The cheesedb command is a command-line tool with one command per feature, and a demo with a real LLM:
go install ./cmd/cheesedb     # puts cheesedb in ~/go/bin (add that folder to your PATH)
cheesedb help                 # every command
cheesedb agent create alice
cheesedb lot alice weather_tool "Pune: rain"
cheesedb demo                 # needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM (see cmd/cheesedb/llm.go)
It keeps its data in ~/.cheesedb (change it with CHEESEDB_DIR). The LLM commands read their server and model from ~/.cheesedb/llm.conf (search adds an embedding model there; see Ask in plain English):
base_url = http://localhost:8000/v1
model    = your-model-name
# api_key = your-key        (only if your server needs one)
The demo tells one story three ways. An agent learns from a user message, a web page and a weather tool. Then the weather tool turns out to be wrong. Here is a real run:
How to read it
- Three sources arrive. Each one is stored as a lot with a label: user_message, web_page, weather_tool.
- The model learns memories and says where each came from. The arrow on the right lists the sources: memory [6] came from [3], the weather tool. Memory [7] was built on [4] and [6].
- Ask a question. The model sees all 4 memories and answers from the weather forecast.
- The weather tool was wrong, so remove source [3] three ways:
  - A, a naive memory list. It deletes the source and nothing else. The model still sees the memories built from it, and gives the same answer.
  - B, cheesedb with Untrusted. One call removes [3] and everything learned from it, [6] and [7]. The model sees only 2 memories, so it no longer knows the forecast. The text is still in the files, and the demo finds the word "rain" in 3 places.
  - C, cheesedb with Erase. The model sees the same 2 memories, and the text is gone from the files. A search of every byte finds nothing.
- The table sums it up: does the model still use the bad data, and is the bad text still on disk?
cheesedb find runs the same byte-by-byte search, so you can check your own data.
cheesedb mcp <agent> serves one agent's memory to any app that speaks the Model Context Protocol (Claude Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop and others), with no code. The app starts it and talks to it over standard input and output; nothing listens on a network port.
cheesedb agent create alice                      # once; the token is saved in ~/.cheesedb/tokens
claude mcp add cheesedb -- cheesedb mcp alice    # Claude Code
For apps with a settings file (Cursor, Claude Desktop), add the same command:
{ "mcpServers": { "cheesedb": { "command": "cheesedb", "args": ["mcp", "alice"] } } }
The model gets five tools, and a sixth, search, when an embedding model is set up (Ask in plain English):
A recall cannot be undone, so recall takes two calls. The first removes nothing: it lists what would be removed and gives a confirm code, and the model is told to show you the list and call again with the code only if you agree. The code fits only that exact list: if anything changes in between, the model gets a new preview instead. If your app supports MCP elicitation (forms a server can show you), the second call also asks you directly, in a form the model cannot fill in, and nothing is removed without your tick. In other apps the two calls are a speed bump, not a lock: a model that ignores its instructions can make both. There, set recall to need your approval in the app's tool permissions.
With an embedding model, the server also tells the model to search before it forgets a memory you describe in words. Search finds memories, not sources: to remove a source, the model recalls the id add_lot gave it.
The agent is fixed by the command line, and no tool takes an agent, so the model cannot switch to another agent through the tools. A tool that fails (an unknown id, a recalled parent) returns its reason to the model, which can correct its next call.
Things to know before you rely on it:
- The model declares the sources and legs itself. A recall is only as complete as the legs it wrote, and a prompt-injected model can declare them wrongly or recall things it should not (see Limits).
- A model that can also run shell commands as you can skip the tools and read every agent's files directly. Isolation holds only when the tools are the model's only way to the data. For real separation, the data would have to belong to another OS user, which is what the planned memory server is for.
- Each tool call opens the store and closes it again, so a second app window or the cheesedb command can use it in between. The cost is the replay time under Limits: small for a young agent, about 0.7 s per call at 1M memories. A search also reloads the index: 9 ms at 1,000 memories, 0.74 s at 100,000, 7.5 s at 1M (How it scales).
- Data lives in ~/.cheesedb, or in CHEESEDB_DIR if the app starts the command with that variable set, as for every cheesedb command.
- Lot: a source the agent learned from (a user message, a web page, a tool result). The caller labels it; cheesedb does not judge sources.
- Memory: something the agent knows.
- Leg: one way a memory was learned. A leg holds while ALL its parents are alive; a memory may have several legs.
- Fair recall: a memory survives while ANY of its legs holds.
- Strict recall: a memory dies if the recalled source is ANYWHERE in its history.
cheesedb enforces these itself; callers cannot get around them through the API:
- a memory always has at least one leg, and is never built on a recalled (dead) parent;
- recall is permanent;
- an agent's handle reaches only that agent's data (isolation by token);
- every write is on disk (fsync) before it is acknowledged, and a crash loses nothing that was acknowledged;
- damaged or edited records are detected (crc, content digest, hash chain);
- a search never returns a recalled lot or memory, and Erase removes their vectors from disk too.
Design: ARCHITECTURE.md. Security: THREAT_MODEL.md. Speed and size, including where cheesedb is slower than SQLite and PostgreSQL: BENCHMARKS.md.
Read these before relying on cheesedb.
Security
- Tamper-evident, not tamper-proof (v1). Anyone who can write the files can: 
  - change a record and rebuild every hash after it;
  - change or remove the newest records;
  - redact a record.
The files alone cannot reveal any of these. Verify() returns a head fingerprint: keep a copy somewhere else, and compare it later to detect them. v2 plans signed records and an external witness.
- Isolation stops mistakes and prompt injection, not the host program. A tool or agent holding Alice's handle cannot reach Bob. But the program that holds the store, or anyone with access to the folder as that OS user, can read every agent's files directly.
- Tokens are shown once. The store keeps only a hash of each token. A lost token cannot be recovered; the agent can only be deleted.
- Over MCP the model is not trusted, but it is powerful. It can add lots, declare legs, and recall (and by default erase) anything in its agent. An app that gives the model a shell lets it bypass the tools altogether. See Use from AI apps.
Data
- Legs are declared by the caller. Recall removes exactly what the declared legs say depends on a source. If a memory was really learned from a source but no leg says so, recalling that source will not remove it.
- Only Erase removes text from disk.
  - Recall(..., Erase) erases the text of the recalled source and of every dead memory below it before returning.
  - Recall(..., Untrusted) hides those memories from the agent, but their text stays in the files until Compact(), which runs only when you call it.
  - Memories still alive through another source keep their text.
- Deleting is not secure erasure. Earlier backups, snapshots and copies keep their data. SSDs and file systems (such as APFS) may keep old blocks after a file is removed.
- Agent names are compared byte by byte. Two names that look the same but are encoded differently in Unicode are two different agents.
Operations
- Damage near the end of an agent's log is cut off, not refused. A crash can leave a half-written batch (up to about 1 MiB) at the end of the active segment, so Open cuts any damage in that last region and reports it in Report.DroppedBytes. Real damage there, even one flipped byte, therefore drops every record after it. In a young agent whose log is under 1 MiB, that can be the whole log. Check Report() after opening. Sealed segments do not have this weakness: damage there is always ErrCorrupt. Batch commit markers could remove it later.
- Windows does not flush directories. Windows rejects Sync on a directory handle ("Access is denied"), so syncDir is a no-op there: a segment or agent folder created, a rename, or a seal file written just before a crash is not guaranteed on disk when the write returns. NTFS journals metadata, so the entry is usually recovered, but the guarantee is weaker than on macOS and Linux. Windows support remains on the roadmap; see issue #26.
- One open store per folder. cheesedb.Open locks the folder; a second process gets cheesedb.ErrLocked until the first calls Close. The lock works on macOS, Linux, the BSDs and Windows, on a local disk. It may not work on network drives (NFS, SMB), and other systems (for example Solaris, AIX) get no lock.
- Startup replays the whole log. It grows with history: about 0.7 s for an agent with 1M memories (BENCHMARKS.md).
- The whole memory graph is kept in RAM: about 205 bytes per memory. An agent's graph must fit in memory.
- About 200 durable writes per second per agent on the test machine, limited by fsync. Different agents write in parallel.
- A damaged agent key file stops the whole store from opening. It is reported rather than skipped, because skipping would hide that agent's data.
- Search is exact, and its index lives in RAM. The index format may still change. Every question is compared with every vector, so search slows as an agent grows; every vector is kept in RAM at one byte per value (about 0.8 KB at 768 values), and the first search after opening reads the whole index from disk. Each cheesedb command and each MCP tool call opens the store again, so at 1M memories every search pays that load (How it scales). No keyword search and no filters yet.
- A damaged index blocks Erase and Compact for that agent until it is dropped, because they could not erase its vectors. So does a dropped index whose folder could not be deleted. The agent itself still opens and works. If a crash interrupted an erase and an index is damaged at the next open, the erase stays pending, text included, until the index is dropped and Compact runs (Report().UnfinishedErase says so).
- The embedding server sees what is remembered and searched. The cheesedb command and MCP server send each new memory's text, and each search question, to the embedding server you set up. A local server keeps them on your machine; a hosted one keeps whatever its provider keeps, and an Erase cannot reach that copy.
- Older versions ignore indexes. If a version without indexes erases a memory, its vectors stay on disk until a current version next loads the index. Do not use an older version on a store with indexes when erasure matters.
Planned work, roughly in order. Plans can change, and nothing here is a promise of a date.
Toward v1.0 (a stable API and on-disk format)
- Windows support. The file lock already works; directory flushing and replacing an open file during Erase are the gaps.
- More fuzzing and crash tests. The record decoder already has a fuzz test. Still to do: feed damaged and truncated files to Open, and kill the process mid-write, to check recovery.
- Independent security review before anything is recommended for real data.
- Batch commit markers, so recovery can tell a half-written last batch from older damage exactly (see Limits).
Next
- Shared memory between agents. A shared space with named members and roles (read, write, admin), every record showing who wrote it, and a way to carry a recall of a shared memory into the private memories built on it. Design in progress.
- Automatic compaction, for example when dead text passes a size threshold. Today Compact() runs only when you call it.
- Encryption per agent. The record format already reserves a key id for it.
Memory server (v2)
- A server for several programs, over a Unix socket only, with per-agent tokens and access logging.
- Read tracking: what an agent read while answering becomes part of what its new memories depend on.
- Trust levels per source type, set by a rule table you configure.
- Signed records and signed head fingerprints, sent to an outside witness, so edits by someone with file access can be detected (see Limits).
- The MCP server moves onto the memory server, so several apps share one running process.
Search (v2.5)
- Faster search for large agents: keeping the index loaded between MCP calls, a lighter load, and an approximate index (IVF).
- Keyword search, and search that combines keywords with meaning.
- Sources in the search index, so forget can find a source by description too.
Scale (v3)
- Snapshots, so opening an agent loads a saved state and replays only newer records, instead of the whole log.
- Concurrent writers across agents, and log-shipping replication checked by the hash chain.
Under consideration (candidates we are weighing, not commitments; each needs a design first)
- Lossless compaction for long conversations. Store every message and tool result as a source, and make a conversation's summary a memory linked to them. A detail the summary dropped can then be pulled back exactly, and recalling a message also removes every summary built from it. Long agent sessions today lose earlier details when they are summarized to fit the context window.
- Superseding outdated facts. "I moved to Mumbai" retires "lives in Pune" and everything built on it, with a record of why, instead of both staying and contradicting each other.
- Blast radius and trace. For a source: every memory it shaped, before or after a recall. For a memory: the sources behind it. Also as MCP tools, so a model can find and recall a source it did not save in the same conversation.
- Source versions. When a document is updated, or access to it is revoked, the answers and summaries built from it become stale or are removed, instead of lingering in caches.
- Timestamps and model version on records, for traceability rules such as the EU AI Act's logging duty, while Erase still removes the content.
- A memory-mapped vector file, so the command and the MCP server search without reloading the whole index on every call.
- Session summaries for MCP apps that cannot hand cheesedb whole conversations.
"Lot" and "recall" are food-safety words. A cheese maker records which milk lots went into which wheels, so when one lot turns out to be contaminated, they recall exactly the cheese made from it. cheesedb does the same for what an agent remembers.

articles.title: Show HN: OpenTodo – a self-hosted, local-first task manager in one Go binary
articles.body:
Plan your day without renting your to-do list.
OpenTodo is a free, open-source to-do app you run on your own server or have hosted for you. It works on your phone and your computer, even offline, shares lists with your family or your team, and keeps your data with you.
Try the demo · Install · Docs · Website
New: OpenTodo for iPhone and iPad is in the App Store. It's the first release, a first step: it connects to your OpenTodo server and adds reminders on the phone, the share sheet, a Today widget and Face ID unlock. Expect some rough edges; tell us what to improve.
Ways to run it: PikaPods (hosted, no server needed) · Docker · Umbrel (coming soon) · Unraid · Home Assistant · Kubernetes (Helm) · Single binary · iPhone and iPad app (App Store) · Android app (APK from GitHub; Google Play and F-Droid coming soon) · all 20 platforms
Type a task the way you say it: Call Sarah next Wed 3pm #work p1 sets the date, time, project and priority. Dictate it, send a page from your phone's share menu or the browser extension (Chrome, Firefox), or forward an email. Anything without a home lands in the Inbox. Quick add · Voice · Capture
Today shows what is due and what is still open from earlier. Give tasks an estimate and drag them onto the Day or Week calendar to see whether the day fits. Today · Time blocking
Open one task in Focus and start a Pomodoro, Flowtime or countdown timer. The time is logged to the task. Focus
Share a project with your family or your team as viewer, editor or admin. Assign tasks, comment, and see what changed. Everyone can edit offline. Sharing
- Your data stays yours. Everything lives in one folder on your server. Export it at any time, import it anywhere, and schedule backups, encrypted if you like, to disk, S3 or WebDAV. Backups · Import and export
- Works offline on every device. Each phone and computer keeps a full copy, so the app works with no connection and syncs when it's back. Install the app
- Bring your tasks. Import from Todoist, TickTick, Things, Super Productivity, Microsoft To Do, Apple Reminders and more, with a preview and undo. Import
- Private by design. No telemetry, no analytics, no third-party scripts. Turn on end-to-end encryption and the server holds only ciphertext. Privacy · Encryption
- Bring your own AI, if you want it. Talk to an assistant in the app, or connect the one you already use. Off by default, and every change can be undone. AI
No subscription, no lock-in, no tracking.
✅ yes · ❌ no · ⚠️ partly, or not documented. Todoist and TickTick have a free plan with limits; Things is a one-time purchase per device type. Based on each product's public information as of November 2026. If an entry is wrong, open an issue with a source.
- No install: open the demo and press Try the demo. You get a private copy with sample data, deleted after a few hours.
- On your machine or server: docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -v opentodo-data:/data ghcr.io/opentodoapp/opentodo:stable Open http://localhost:8080. The first visit creates your account. No configuration needed.
git clone https://github.com/OpenTodoApp/OpenTodo.git
cd OpenTodo
docker compose up -d
Data is kept in the opentodo-data volume. On a server reachable from the internet, finish setup right after starting it, or set OPENTODO_SETUP_CODE=required (the setup code). Behind a reverse proxy, set OPENTODO_BASE_URL=https://todo.example.com.
The image is published for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. :stable is the latest release, :1 follows every 1.x release, a minor tag such as :1.5 gets that line's fixes only, a full version such as :1.5.0 pins one release, and :latest follows the main branch. Upgrades from any release since 0.1.0 work directly, and nothing you rely on breaks within 1.x (stability). More in Running with Docker.
Download opentodo-<os>-<arch> for Linux, macOS or Windows from the latest release and run it. It serves on port 8080 and keeps its data in ./data. To build from source: make build && ./bin/opentodo (Go 1.26+ and Node 22+).
Managed hosting: PikaPods, Railway. These links support the project: OpenTodo receives a share when you host through them.
Nothing is required. Every setting is an optional environment variable with a safe default: see the configuration reference. To add people, keep sign-up closed and send invitation links (managing users).
The self-hosting handbook covers every platform, TLS, backups, upgrades and monitoring. The ot command-line client is in the CLI guide.
The app talks only to your own server: no analytics, crash reporters, update pings or third-party fonts. Two things are on by default and can be turned off: maps for task locations, fetched through your server with no account data, and web push to the service each phone's browser chose. Everything else the server contacts, such as webhooks, backup destinations, single sign-on, email or an AI provider, is something you set up. The audit log never records task content (what is logged).
Read the docs with screenshots and search at open-todo.app/docs, or in the app under Help. The same pages are in docs/.
- Start here: getting started · all user guides
- Self-hosting: handbook · configuration · backups
- Build on it: REST API · OpenAPI description · CLI · AI and agents · stability
- Project: changelog · roadmap · security
Every server describes its API at /api/v1/openapi.json (OpenAPI 3.1, generated from the code, stable through 1.x). Point a generator at it and you have a typed client:
curl -s https://todo.example.com/api/v1/openapi.json -o openapi.json
npx openapi-typescript openapi.json -o opentodo.d.ts
The same file is docs/openapi.json and an asset of every release. Sign in with an API token from Settings → Integrations → API tokens; the API guide has the details, and ot, the Obsidian plugin and the n8n nodes are clients built on it.
Under the hood
┌───────────────────────── device ─────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────── server ────────────┐
│ React PWA  ──►  IndexedDB (source of truth)              │      │ Go binary + SQLite             │
│                 │ every edit = field ops {ts, device}    │ sync │  ops log (append-only)         │
│                 └► outbox ──────────────────────────────►├─────►│  fields (last-writer-wins)     │
│                 ◄─ ops from other devices ◄──────────────┤◄─────┤  REST, CalDAV, email, import   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │  all write through ops         │
                                                                  └────────────────────────────────┘
- Every change is a small operation that sets one field of one entity, stamped with a hybrid logical clock and the device id.
- Devices apply changes locally first, then sync. The same per-field rule runs everywhere, so all devices agree no matter the order. Notes merge character by character.
- The REST API, CalDAV, email and imports write through the same log, so a task created with curl shows up on your phone right away.
- One Go binary with the web app inside and a single SQLite file. It idles at about 20 MB of memory and runs on a Raspberry Pi.
More in architecture and the sync protocol.
- Star and share. A star on GitHub helps other people find OpenTodo.
- Leave feedback in Discussions or on Discord.
- Report bugs in issues.
- Review a translation. The app speaks eight languages; tell us where a word feels wrong (translating).
- Test it on your devices and report back in the call for testers.
- Answer questions from other people in Discussions and on Discord.
- Sponsor: buy me a coffee or GitHub Sponsors.
To contribute code, read CONTRIBUTING.md: changes that alter behaviour start as an OpenSpec change. Security issues go to the address in SECURITY.md.
OpenTodo is free and always will be. If it helps you, you can buy a coffee or sponsor it; the support page says what it costs to run and where the money goes.
Thank you to everyone who keeps OpenTodo going. Supporters who want to be listed appear here.
AGPL-3.0-only. You can run, study, modify and share OpenTodo freely. If you offer a modified version as a network service, you must offer its source under the same license. That is what keeps a self-hosted project from being quietly turned back into a subscription.

A reproducer that triggers this within seconds instead of minutes or hours,
in case it helps test the fix. As root, on an ext4 filesystem:
  d=$(mktemp -d /var/tmp/repro.XXXXXX)
  for i in $(seq 100); do head -c 262144 /dev/urandom > "$d/f$i"; done; sync
  echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches

in that block group oopses (the NULL folio from __filemap_get_folio() in
ext4_mb_load_buddy_gfp()). WARNING: on an affected kernel this hangs every
writer on that filesystem; only a power cycle recovers. On 6.1.190-1 it

Hello,
Another data point for this bug, in case it helps.
Two Debian 12 KVM guests (virtio-scsi, ext4 root, Docker with
overlay2),
running on different physical hosts, froze after upgrading to
linux-image-6.1.0-55-amd64 (6.1.192-1). There were four freezes in
total.
Every freeze started right after an hourly cron job
"sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches": the last journal/syslog
entry
each time was "drop_caches: 3", at the first run after each boot
(roughly 10 to 55 minutes after boot). After that, disk I/O blocked
completely: journald stopped writing, processes were stuck in D state
and
systemd watchdog timeouts followed. The kernel itself kept running
(netfilter messages on the console, ICMP replies). No oops reached the
journal.
On 6.1.0-54 (6.1.190-1) the same job ran hourly for weeks without
problems, and it still completes normally today.
Both machines are in production, so I am not able to reproduce the
freeze on 6.1.192-1 to capture the oops. I am running 6.1.0-54 for
now,
will test 6.1.192-2 once it is available, and will report back.
Thank you for the quick work on this.
